data.title: Jim Ratcliffe rescues vital British plastics factory from collapse
data.description:
Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the billionaire boss of Ineos, has rescued Britain’s last factory producing critical chemicals used in the UK plastics industry.

Ineos confirmed on Friday that it had rescued Runcorn MCP, the UK’s last producer of ethylene dichloride, which is used to make PVC.

The vital plastic is used for making water pipes, electrical cable, medical tubing and window frames, making it crucial for the construction industry.

Ineos Inovyn, the chemicals giant’s chlorine arm, said it had bought a 50pc shareholding in Runcorn MCP together with its assets and staff from Vynova Runcorn, which entered administration last year, putting dozens of jobs at risk.

Ethylene dichloride is made from petrochemicals originating from crude oil. Up to 15pc of all the oil used in the UK goes into the production of raw materials, such as plastics.

Stephen Dossett, the chief executive of Ineos Inovyn, said: “Chlor-alkali products are essential to modern life, supporting safe drinking water, pharmaceuticals and healthcare, and the materials that underpin housing and critical infrastructure.

“This acquisition is an important step in strengthening the UK’s national resilience.”

Ineos already has sites in Runcorn making chemicals including chlorine – used to purify much of the UK’s drinking water as well as in producing a range of chemicals. It also produces salt, caustic soda and other products.

Around 98pc of the chlorine used in drinking water is supplied from Runcorn.

The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, comes amid escalating concerns that Britain’s industrial base is being destroyed by the UK’s high energy costs and carbon taxes.

The chemicals industry has been a major casualty of the country’s soaring energy costs, shrinking by 20pc in the past three years.

Sir Jim warned last year that the chemicals industry in Europe was facing “extinction” from the cost of “enormously high energy prices and crippling carbon tax bills”.

Sir Jim, who also owns a minority stake in Manchester United, issued a further warning about the state of the UK’s energy policy last month.

He said: “We’ve had seven prime ministers in 10 years and they all come in with a new idea of how best to run our energy policy in the UK.

“Now we’ve got another one and heaven knows what direction we’re going to turn in now.

“There’s no point in investing and then finding we get our ninth prime minister.”

data.title: How to choose the best children’s savings accounts for 2026
data.description:
A children’s savings account works in a very similar way to an adult one. You can open many of these accounts for children under the age of 18 with as little as £1. Seeing the balance grow is a good way to teach children financial skills as many accounts allow children over the age of seven to add and withdraw money themselves.

You can choose between an easy or instant-access, fixed term or a regular savings account. Easy or instant-access accounts allow you to withdraw or deposit money at any time, but they usually have lower interest rates. Regular savings accounts can require you to save every month and the withdrawals may not be as straightforward. They generally pay higher interest, but this can be reduced if you miss a monthly deposit.

In this guide, we will cover:

  • How we determine the best rates
  • The best children’s savings accounts in September
  • Expert opinion: Things to consider when choosing an account for your child
  • How to open a children’s savings account
  • Children’s savings account vs Junior Isa
  • Children’s savings accounts FAQs

How we determine the best rates

The Best Buy tables show the best savings rates widely available in the market. This means certain accounts are excluded, including those that require minimum deposits of more than £25,000 or are available only to local or existing customers.

The data in these tables is provided by Savings Data Limited and is compiled using automated tracker tools and updates from savings providers. Savings Data Limited then manually checks the information and enters it into a database that feeds the live tables, which update daily.

The savings accounts shown are protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme. The information in this article is intended for information purposes and should not be taken as endorsement or advice.

The best children’s savings accounts in September

The table below highlights the best savings accounts you can open for your children.

For more ways to save for your child, check out our guide to the best Junior cash Isas.

If you’re looking for a new home for your own savings, you can find the best tax-efficient options in our guide to cash Isas, while our pick of easy access savings accounts can reveal the best options if you want to add and withdraw money whenever you like.

Alternatively, you may be able to find higher rates if you’re willing to lock your cash away for a year or more – the top rates are in our guide to the best fixed-rate bonds.

Expert opinion: Things to consider when choosing an account for your child

  • What type of account suits you best?
  • What’s the interest rate?
  • Is it suitable for your child’s age?
  • Is it easy to manage?
  • Are there any restrictive terms for deposits and withdrawals?

Caitlyn Eastell, of analyst Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, said: “There are many children’s savings accounts to choose from, ranging from easy access, regular savers or Junior Isas. They are a good option for parents wishing to save for their child’s future.”

But she reminded savers of the tax implications: “It is worth noting that children are still liable to pay tax and have the same personal allowance as adults and once the child reaches a certain age, usually 18, the account will automatically roll into an adult savings account, where they will have full control.”

Mark Hicks, of stockbroker Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “Children’s accounts are brilliant but are not advertised enough. I think the UK still has a big problem in that financial education, particularly in schools, is not on the agenda. So getting a child an account and encouraging them to save from a young age is incredibly important.”

What makes a good children’s savings account?

  • A good savings rate: This might seem obvious, but the money you save for your children will grow and compound at a much faster rate if you can make sure the interest rate is competitive. If possible, it should at least match inflation – otherwise the money will be losing value in real terms.
  • Easy to manage: Consider whether you’ll need the option to make withdrawals, how you want to open and manage the account, and whether there are decent options when your child gets older – for instance, does the provider offer accounts for teenagers to help them manage their money?
  • Suits your savings plans: Many children’s accounts can be opened with £1, and may have fairly low maximum deposits. However, these won’t be suitable if you have a more significant amount to save.
  • Suitable for your child’s age: Watch out for minimum and maximum age requirements as this may affect when you can start saving for your child, and how long you can save for.

How to open a children’s savings account

  1. Choose an account: Weighing up the factors explained above, choose a provider and account that suits you and your child.
  2. Check the small print: Just in case there are any restrictions or details that aren’t obvious, comb the terms and conditions for anything that might make you change your mind.
  3. Go with your opening method of choice: Once you’re happy, go and open the account. Some providers let you open an account online or you may have to visit a branch or do it by post. Providers may have their own rules for how old a child needs to be to open an account under their own name, and young children, often under eight, typically need a parent to sign and set one up on their behalf. You may need to provide documents such as a birth certificate for the child and your own ID.
  4. Start saving: You may be able to save into your child’s account via online payments or bank transfers. If your child receives money from friends and family, such as on their birthday, you may also be able to get them involved by taking them to a branch to make a cash deposit. Be sure to take note of any deposit restrictions.

Managing your child’s account

Some accounts let children manage the account themselves from a certain age, depending on whether they were made a signatory when it was opened.

In some cases, even if the child can manage the account, they may need to have a parent or guardian with them when they visit the bank to request changes, or withdraw money.

Children’s accounts usually convert to an adult savings account once the child turns 18, but there is more flexibility before that and you may be able to access the funds if needed.

Are child’s savings accounts taxed?

Children don’t usually have to pay tax on savings interest – but it’s not because they can’t be taxed. Since children don’t usually have any other forms of income, the amount earned from savings interest rarely exceeds the combined amount of their personal allowance and personal savings allowance (PSA).

But if a parent is contributing money into the account and it earns more than £100, this will go towards their own personal savings allowance.

If you are worried about this, another type of child savings account is the Junior Isa.

This has a separate annual £9,000 allowance to the adult Isa that can be put into a cash or stocks and shares Isa for children to access after the turn 18. All growth is tax-free – for both children and parents.

Children’s savings account vs Junior Isa

  • Product choice: There are generally more children’s savings account to choose from than Junior Isas, and interest rates can be higher for savings accounts.
  • Tax: Interest or investment growth in Junior Isas is tax-free, but interest earned in a children’s savings account is taxable.
  • Access: No money can be withdrawn from a Junior Isa. With these accounts, the money is locked away until the child becomes an adult. At this point, the account will convert to an adult Isa, and they will get full control of it. Many children’s savings accounts will allow withdrawals, which can be a useful way to teach children about the value of money.
  • Type of account: Children’s savings account just save in cash, but with a Junior Isa parents can choose to save in cash or invest with a stocks and shares option for their child.

Children’s savings accounts FAQs

Grandparents may be able to open a savings account for their grandchildren, as long as they bring proof of identity, such as a birth certificate. You usually need permission from the parents.

The cash from a grandparent won’t be taxed at the point it was given, though it could be caught by inheritance tax depending on when the gift was made.

Parents and step-parents can become liable for tax on their child’s savings interest, so it’s something to keep an eye on.

If over £100 interest or dividends is earned on the money you give a child, the interest will be taxed as if it were yours. This does not apply to Junior Isas or child trust funds.

This rule only applies to parents – friends and grandparents can give as much as they like without worrying about the interest.

As for the possibility of children paying tax on savings interest, that could also happen – but it’s much less likely. As with adults, children are liable for tax and have a personal allowance of £12,570, plus a £5,000 starting savings allowance and a £1,000 personal savings allowance. If annual income, including interest, exceeds the personal allowance, then income tax will be due.

This depends on the account and the age of the child. Generally, if your child is under eight the account is held in trust by the adult who opened it. Some accounts allow the parent to remain the signatory until your child is 16.

Many accounts let children take control of their savings from the age of seven, meaning they can deposit and withdraw money.

As a parent, you can open a savings account for your child from when they’re born – doing so means you can get saving for them straightaway, so their money can grow and compound over the longest time possible.

Certain accounts will have specific age restrictions – particularly those that offer some form of access for your child. These can be great when your children get a bit older, commonly from around age seven, as a way to teach them about saving and the value of money. Providers will be able to advise what age restrictions are applicable for specific accounts.

data.title: The hotels hiring robots to cut their wage bills
data.description:
The reception workers at the Henn na – or “Weird” – Hotel gaze blankly at guests.

Some of the uncanny staff members look like Japanese women. Others are talking Velociraptors. All of them are robots.

In fact, the novelty Tokyo hotel is known for being the first in the world to be “run by” machines. They speak different languages and carry out front-of-house tasks such as greetings, check-in and tourist information.

Bosses have claimed the robots could eventually yield savings of 75pc on labour costs.

Tellingly, however, the hotel still relies on a small army of human “stagehands” for the important jobs that require the most manpower. They take care of mishaps, tidy up bedrooms, water the plants and keep hard-to-reach areas free of cobwebs.

Until now, deploying robots has seemed more like a gimmick than a serious strategy to hospitality bosses, who aren’t interested in using machines that will only slow them down.

Yet with the technology improving rapidly, many are now re-examining how automation could shake up the industry.

One veteran executive says this is primarily being driven by labour costs, which have surged in Europe and the US.

Travelodge said last year that it aimed to partly mitigate £21m of higher costs – resulting from a rising minimum wage and increasing employer National Insurance contributions – by ramping up its use of robot vacuum cleaners across its estate.

Technology also allows hotels to provide a more personalised offering and experiences focused on “wellness”.

“Sleep and wellbeing are also becoming more mainstream consumer priorities,” the executive says. “Fundamentally, what hotels are selling is a good night’s sleep.”

Along with devices such as self-service kiosks, more futuristic gadgets are starting to appear.

In Newcastle, the Maldron Hotel claims to have doubled room service revenues by introducing a wheeled “ButlerBot” that delivers food and other treats directly to a guest’s door.

One start-up riding the wave towards high-tech personalisation is Nook, founded by Piers Millar, a young British entrepreneur.

He argues that the modern hotel room should follow the example of Waymo’s driverless taxis in San Francisco, California, which allow passengers to set the car’s temperature and play their own music – with these preferences automatically remembered when they next hail a vehicle.

“We really want to drive efficiency through technology but it’s also about giving people a much more personalised experience,” Millar says.

His company’s big idea is to repeat the trick in the hotel business. Since the start of August, it has been trialling a concept room at the Superhero Hotel, formerly the Commodore, in San Francisco and it has signed a deal to open in London as well.

Guests can select their preferred lighting, music and temperatures of their room and mattress before they check in, so it’s all set up when they arrive.

The bed also collects data on your heart rate and sleep quality and will optimise itself over time to ensure a better rest.

Millar ultimately wants to build a new hotel chain where automation will allow staff to ditch the drudgery and focus more on guests.

The company’s next frontier, housekeeping, remains largely untouched by automation. It is also the biggest labour cost for hotel owners.

In major hotel chains, a housekeeper will spend anywhere between 20 and 45 minutes turning around a room once a guest has checked out.

The prize from any time savings here could be substantial, with even a few minutes per room adding up to potentially major cost savings.

However, there are still some basic obstacles to an automated cleaning revolution. For instance, robot vacuum cleaners must still be let into rooms manually by humans.

Likewise, cleaning a hotel-room bathroom is a tricky task for robots. But options for automation do exist.

For instance, self-cleaning toilet cubicles are now commonplace in some European cities such as Paris.

These “superloos” function similarly to dishwashers, with the door locking automatically after a person exits and a wash cycle cleaning and drying the entire toilet fixture and floor.

Millar believes they could be the best solution for hotels, although the significant plumbing means they cannot easily be retrofitted to older hotels.

Another area with potential is bedding. In budget hotels, it takes about 20 minutes to clean a room, with changing the bed taking up up to half of this time.

But Millar and his team at Nook are developing a “self-changing” bed that will be able to strip itself, with a housekeeper then only required to clip on new sheets.

Similar shifts towards robots are starting to happen in other parts of the hospitality industry as well.

British start-up Kaikaku has been pioneering industrial kitchen appliances and software that speed up the production of food.

It has started out with a conveyor-belt system that makes fresh salad bowls but in future will target other products such as burgers.

Josef Chen, its chief executive, says: “You want to target restaurants where the bulk of revenue is coming from a single product that is made through a very repetitive process.

“The idea is that eventually, everything could be so automated that there’s nothing left for staff to focus on except the customers.”

Kaikaku was recently acquired by Reef, an American tech firm backed by Japanese giant SoftBank.

The company says its machines can cut labour costs by 70pc and make 360 salad bowls an hour – equivalent to one every 10 seconds.

This sort of technology is particularly attractive to hotels and restaurants that have faced significant tax rises under Labour, says Allen Simpson, the chief executive of UKHospitality.

However, he fears the sector is under such strain that many venues will end up laying off humans.

“You want to be in a situation where the robots take out the lower-productivity work,” he says. “But we’re actually in a position where the robots just take the job and the person isn’t redeployed because the employer can’t afford it.”

However, while there are clearly jobs that robots can handle that don’t require a human touch – such as the robo-butlers in Newcastle – many guests still expect a human face in hospitality.

Simpson points to two cocktail bars that recently opened in south London. One was run by two passionate bartenders who made their drinks the usual way, while the other was automated and sold canned cocktails.

“The canned bar went bust really quickly because – even though a Negroni is just three ingredients mixed together – people still want a human to have mixed their drink.”

data.title: Volkswagen faces ‘more than critical’ crisis, warns carmaker’s boss
data.description:
Volkswagen’s chief executive has warned that the crisis facing the German carmaker is “more than critical”, urging employees to brace for “the biggest upheaval in their history”.

Oliver Blume said US tariffs, the war in the Middle East and mounting competition from China had all contributed to a downturn that threatens to worsen in the coming years.

In an internal memo seen by The Telegraph, he said that Volkswagen’s current profits were “by no means sufficient” for it to continue investing in “new technologies, new products and our locations”.

He added that “we have to assume that risks will get worse, worldwide”, claiming that “we are in the biggest transformation in the history of the global automotive industry”.

His comments form part of efforts to win over staff as part of a controversial turnaround plan, which could include closing four of its German factories and laying off as many as 100,000 workers.

The company’s brands include Audi, Porsche and Škoda.

Mr Blume said that “Chinese manufacturers are pushing aggressively into Europe” and selling cars at “price points we cannot match”.

He added that he could not see any way Volkswagen’s factories in Emden, Hannover, Zwickau and Neckarsulm could remain profitable into the next decade.

The carmaker’s chief said Volkswagen’s overheads were “still around 30pc above the level of comparable companies”, adding: “We cannot carry that disadvantage indefinitely and must reduce it.”

Volkswagen made history in December last year by closing its Dresden plant. This was the first time the carmaker had shut one of its German factories in its 88-year history.

Mr Blume said Volkswagen was also exploring “industrial solutions” to keep its factories running, as he suggested that shutting factories would be “the last and most expensive solution”.

He highlighted the potential to convert Volkswagen’s Osnabrück plant into a production facility for Israeli firm Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, with the aim of saving 2,300 jobs.

Volkswagen first announced plans to cut 50,000 jobs in 2024.

However, the restructuring led to a fierce backlash from Germany’s powerful trade unions who have led protests at its factories across the country.

Mr Blume said Volkswagen had already reached agreements with around 37,000 staff to cut jobs, primarily through early retirement deals.

The carmaker warned last year that Donald Trump’s tariffs would inflict a €5bn- (£4.4bn) a-year hit on its business.

data.title: 160-year-old Devon ‘war metal’ mine to reopen
data.description:
A century-old tungsten mine in Devon is set to restart production after receiving £71m in taxpayer funding.

In the latest effort to boost Britain’s rearmament, the Government’s National Wealth Fund (NWF) has invested in Tungsten West, the owner of Hemerdon mine near Plymouth.

The cash will be used to reopen Hemerdon for the first time in eight years, with the mine boasting some of the largest tungsten reserves in the world.

As part of the deal, the NWF will take a 7pc stake in Tungsten West for £36m before lending the business £35m.

It reflects a drive to make the UK more self-sufficient in critical minerals, particularly metals vital to defence.

Recent conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have sent demand for tungsten surging, which is one of the most dense and heavy metals.

It is used in everything from hypersonic missile nose cones to armour-piercing bullets, bunker-busting bombs and “airburst” counter-drone shells.

John Healey, the new Chancellor, said: “We are living in a more dangerous world, which is why backing British industry is more important than ever before.

“That is what this deal does. We are tapping into one of the largest deposits of tungsten in the world, right here in the UK.”

The Hemerdon mine was first discovered in 1867 and mined during both world wars before closing in 1944.

It was briefly reopened between 2015 and 2018 before shutting again because of a lack of funds.

‘Increasing global demand’

Tungsten West, which is listed on London’s alternative investment market, was founded in 2019 with the aim of reopening the mine, which contains the fourth-largest tungsten reserves in the world.

Oliver Holbourn, the chief of the NWF, said: “There is strong and increasing global demand for tungsten, supported by its strategic applications in defence, next generation energy and aerospace.

“In Hemerdon, the UK has one of the largest deposits of tungsten in the world right on our doorstep.”

Tungsten West is set to start mining tin and tungsten at the Hemerdon mine by the end of this year before returning to full production in early 2027.

China produces roughly 80pc of the world’s tungsten supplies. However, prices of the critical metal have surged in the past year as a result of export restrictions imposed by Beijing.

Britain imports the entirety of its tungsten supplies from countries including France, Germany and China.

However, at full production the Hemerdon mine is expected to produce 3,300 tonnes of tungsten concentrate a year – equivalent to 20pc of world supplies outside China.

Jeff Court, Tungsten West’s chief executive, said: “Hemerdon is a world-class, low-cost and long-life tungsten and tin resource in the UK.

“It is extremely important to us that we prioritise UK requirements for this critical metal to support domestic demand, including strategic initiatives across defence and next generation energy.”

data.title: Florida’s housing market goes into meltdown
data.description:
When the owner of a three-bedroom townhouse in Orlando’s 300-acre Margaritaville resort, a master-planned estate near the Walt Disney World Resort, sold the property earlier this year, he was in for a nasty shock.

He had purchased the newly built home for $710,000 (£525,000) in 2022 as a short-term buy-to-let investment, seeking to cash in on booming demand from both holidaymakers and families relocating to Florida in the wake of the pandemic.

Since then, the market has undergone a sea change. When the investor sold up this year, he received just $340,000 – less than half what he paid four years ago.

The sharp drop in price put him firmly in negative equity and he had to pay several hundred thousand dollars to his bank to settle the debt.

But the bill would have been even bigger if he had waited, warns James Donovan, the owner of Team Donovan brokers, which conducted the transaction.

“That was six months ago,” he says. “Now, I’m negotiating on a property with the same kind of floor plan, and we’re talking a price of around $300,000.”

This is just the tip of the iceberg. While prices are holding up at the luxury end of Florida’s property market, mainstream real estate in the Sunshine State has gone into meltdown.

For two or three years in the wake of the pandemic, Florida’s property market boomed as a tidal wave of buyers raced to relocate or invest in holiday lets. Prices soared and developers accelerated construction.

But the surge in demand was finite. Immigration has since plummeted. Sky-high mortgage rates, which have climbed from 3pc in 2021 to 6.66pc today, are hammering local buyer affordability. And falling occupancy rates in short-term lets mean that Airbnb investors can no longer secure the rents they need to make their sums add up.

This has meant significant price discounts, falling transactions, a rising number of distressed sellers – and a brewing headache for Donald Trump, the US president, before crucial midterm elections in November.

“The homeowners I’m dealing with now who bought in 2022 are selling for between $50,000 and $350,000 less than they bought for,” says Donovan.

Nick Gerli, the chief executive of Reventure App, a housing market analytics tool, says: “There’s a national housing recession in the US. A lack of affordability on prices combined with higher mortgage rates, which is nuking housing demand.”

But this is far from Florida’s only problem. “What’s different in Florida is that not only is the demand down but supply is way up,” Gerli adds.

Data from Realtor.com show that the number of homes listed for sale in Florida surged by 110pc between 2023 and 2025 to hit the highest level in a decade.

The state, which accounts for 7pc of the US population, is currently home to 15pc of the country’s property listings.

A wave of short-term let investors who piled into the market from 2020 to 2022 are trying to exit because they are no longer receving the rental returns, says Gerli.

He adds: “A lot of regular Americans went on Instagram during the pandemic and read about how they could quit their job and have a six-figure passive income operating Airbnbs. It is just no longer true.”

Figures from AirDNA, which scrapes short-term lettings sites, show the number of short-term rental listings across Florida has surged by 22pc since July 2019. But occupancy rates have declined from 69.1pc to 67.5pc during the same period.

In purpose-built resort communities, homeowners struggling to sell up must compete with housebuilders who are scrambling to shift a substantial pipeline of inventory.

Florida currently has 10 months of new-build supply. This means that, if nothing new were added to the market, it would take nearly a year to sell the available inventory.

“That is reaching financial crisis levels of new construction,” says Jon Brooks, the co-founder of Momentum Realty.

Housebuilders are not only offering six-figure price discounts, they are often paying between $20,000 and $50,000 per property to reduce the mortgage rates.

Builders can do this by purchasing bulk pools of so-called forward commitments, which give them access to a certain interest rate through a lender for a limited period.

“They use whatever tactic is possible,” says Brooks. “We’ve even seen people say, ‘Hey! If you buy this house, we’ll give you a golf cart.’ There are all of these perks to try to get the buyer to basically overpay.”

Across Florida, Redfin figures show sales are down by 20pc compared with 2019 levels. Home values have slumped by 7pc since 2024 to a five-year low of $378,166 according to Zillow.

Distress is mounting. So far this year, 1.2pc of transactions in central Florida were either bank repossessions or short sales, whereby the bank agrees to share losses with a borrower who sells while they are in negative equity, says Donovan.

The number is still well below the pre-pandemic figure of 3.3pc, but it is climbing. This was up from 0.5pc in 2022, and was the first time in six years that the share has exceeded 1pc.

Many new homeowners made their purchase using Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans, which are government-backed and require borrowers to commit to down-payments of only 3.5pc. This means it only takes a small price fall for their home to be worth less than they borrowed to pay for it.

National delinquency rates on FHA loans, which make up 16pc of all outstanding mortgages and are heavily concentrated among lower earners, have surged to nearly 12pc. This was up from 8pc before the pandemic. Excluding the Covid surge, the number is now at a 14-year high.

Justin Begley, an economist at Moody’s Analytics, says: “Given that living costs are typically at the top of household budget priorities, rising home-loan delinquencies signal an extraordinarily high level of financial stress by those who hold those loans.”

What is happening on the ground in Florida is a reflection of America’s so-called K-shaped economy. While those at the top end of the income spectrum are seeing their riches grow, those at the bottom are becoming increasingly overwhelmed by the cost of living and debt.

It is a problem that is mounting in urgency for Trump before the midterms. The president made endless promises on the campaign trail to bring down the cost of living. He knows that even rural Maga voters are now growing impatient to see results.

In Florida, the housing crisis will bring back unwelcome memories of 2007, when the state was the epicentre of the subprime mortgage crisis that triggered the global financial crisis.

By 2010, a staggering 68pc of sales in central Florida were either bank repossessions or short sales, says Donovan. Between 2007 and 2012, prices fell across the state by 50pc.

Analysts argue that banks and housebuilders are not vulnerable in the way that they were back then. Regulations introduced in the wake of the credit crunch mean mortgage providers have much higher-quality loan books.

“I don’t think we’re going to see another 50pc drop. But could we see a 20pc correction across the state and some individual listings down more than 50pc?” says Gerli. “I think that’s a reasonable possibility with the current trajectory.”

data.title: Former BBC director Tim Davie joins French TV company
data.description:
The former BBC boss has taken up a new role at a French TV giant after leaving the embattled broadcaster.

Tim Davie has joined the board of Mediawan, the production group behind shows including Slow Horses and Call My Agent!.

Mediawan operates a network of more than 100 production companies with a combined annual spend of more than $2bn (£1.5bn).

It has been growing through a string of acquisitions in recent months, including Peter Chernin’s North Road Company and Brad Pitt’s Plan B, which was behind Netflix’s Adolescence.

The Paris-based production group is also mooted as a potential suitor for ITV’s production business, which is set to be carved out from the broadcaster after the sale of its channels to Sky.

Mr Davie, who stepped down as director-general of the BBC in April, is also joining FGS Global, the public-relations firm whose UK operations were founded by Roland Rudd. FGS’s list of clients includes a number of major blue-chip companies.

Both Mediawan and FGS are backed by KKR, the US private equity giant that has invested in a string of British firms including broadband provider Hyperoptic and Northumbrian Water.

Mr Davie’s appointments, which were first reported by Sky News, signal a return to corporate life for the former BBC boss, whose tenure at the public service broadcaster was underpinned by a push to generate more commercial revenues.

The former PepsiCo executive had previously led BBC Studios, the corporation’s commercial arm, and he sought to expand this part of the business through advertising and licensing deals around the world in an effort to offset declining income from the licence fee.

However, Mr Davie’s time at the BBC was marred by a string of scandals.

These included the BBC’s broadcasting of chants of “death, death to the IDF” during Bob Vylan’s Glastonbury set last summer and a Gaza documentary that breached the corporation’s guidelines.

The BBC was also engulfed in misconduct scandals surrounding high-profile presenters, including Huw Edwards, who pleaded guilty to three counts of making indecent images of children, and Gregg Wallace, who was sacked in the wake of allegations of historical misconduct, which he denies.

Mr Davie was ultimately forced to resign after the BBC aired a misleading edit of Donald Trump’s speech before the 2021 Capitol riot. The broadcaster is fighting a $10bn defamation lawsuit filed by the US president.

In addition to his new corporate roles, Mr Davie last month took up the role of co-chairman of the Government’s Creative Industries Council.

The former BBC boss will become sole chairman from next year, when Baroness Vadera of Holland Park, his fellow co-chairman, steps down.

Matt Brittin, Mr Davie’s successor and a former Google executive, is pushing ahead with bruising cost-cutting that could lead to up to 2,000 people – or 10pc of the BBC’s workforce – losing their jobs.

He is also locked in discussions with ministers about the future of the licence fee as the BBC’s Royal Charter comes up for renewal.

In a damning assessment of the BBC’s prospects, Amol Rajan, the outgoing Today programme presenter, said last week the broadcaster was “screwed” unless the licence fee funding model was replaced.

data.title: White House hits out at Labour over media ‘censorship’ plans
data.description:
Donald Trump’s White House has accused Labour of censorship over its plans to promote “trusted” news online.

The US embassy in London said proposals to force tech giants to promote news from certain media outlets raised “serious” concerns about free speech.

It warned that a plan to give the Government influence over which news sources citizens see online “risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship”.

Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, has outlined proposals to force tech firms such as Google, Facebook and X to prominently display news from public-service broadcasters such as the BBC, ITV and Channel 4.

Ministers have not explained how media outlets would qualify as “trusted” under the scheme, which could also be extended to local and national newspapers.

The White House said the move would harm independent journalism and warned the effect on any outlets that did not receive “trusted” status was “not meaningfully different than outright removal”.

It said the US government would “likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship”, adding that any such measures could create a template for authoritarian regimes.

Ministers have refused to rule out requiring news publishers to submit to a state-backed regulator such as Impress, which was set up in the wake of the Leveson inquiry into phone hacking.

Andy Burnham previously called for a second phase of the inquiry, while he was joined on his by-election campaign by actors Hugh Grant and Steve Coogan, who are vocal supporters of the press reform group Hacked Off.

The US intervention suggests Labour risks fresh tensions with the Trump administration, which has previously attacked the UK over its approach to free speech and tighter regulation of tech giants.

The proposals form part of wider efforts to counteract a deluge of online misinformation and disinformation and to protect news publishers from a decline in traffic triggered by Google’s search changes and AI tools.

But any effort to tie prominence to tighter regulation has triggered fears that the Government would control what news people see online and be able to exert influence over the press.

The News Media Association – which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian – said the proposed measures risked “narrowing the range of trusted voices available to people across the country”.

Officials have insisted that the measures would protect the plurality of news sources in the UK.

The White House said the changes could have a knock-on effect on what its users see around the world, adding: “The US government has made clear its opposition to measures resulting in extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online.”

The Trump administration also warned that any effort to promote British news outlets above others raised competition concerns and would place an unfair burden on US companies, especially after ministers introduced increased protections for so-called recognised news publishers under new online safety laws.

It said: “We encourage the UK to consider how prescriptive design mandates that boost ‘trustworthy news’ could affect the UK’s reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation – rather than one that unduly constrains the development and use of technology.”

A spokesman for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper.

“We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”

data.title: Richard Branson’s plan to make the Eurostar feel like a second-class service
data.description:
Sir Richard Branson’s much touted plan to bring some of the glamour of Virgin Atlantic to his own version of the Eurostar has been derided as a pipe dream by critics.

Overcrowding at St Pancras, a chronic lack of suitable train-maintenance sites and the inevitable mountain of red tape have been viewed as almost insurmountable obstacles to anyone intent on ending Eurostar’s monopoly over services through the Channel tunnel.

But after securing permission to run 20 trains a day between London and the Continent from Britain’s rail regulator, the billionaire’s Virgin Trains is finally beginning to win over doubters.

Virgin must still negotiate access to the tunnel itself, as well as tracks in France, Belgium and the Netherlands. And it faces a nervous wait for a fleet of 12 as yet untested high-speed trains on order from manufacturer Alstom.

However, a ruling from regulators at the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) last week suggests Sir Richard may be about to make good on his ambition of returning to Britain’s railways after Virgin Trains lost the West Coast Main Line franchise in 2019.

Virgin Trains is not the only operator intent on challenging Eurostar’s 31-year monopoly.

Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia announced earlier this month a €2bn (£1.7bn) order for 19 new trains, around half of which it aims to deploy on Channel tunnel services, while a clutch of other would-be operators are also drawing up proposals.

If those plans come to fruition, competition on the route could explode within five years, which could have an impact matching that of the 1990s discount-airline boom.

Plunging fares may encourage an influx of new customers and further loosen the grip of airlines on routes such as London to Paris, where Eurostar already has 80pc of the market.

Train services from London are likely to reach further into Europe, with lower ticket prices making rail competitive as far as Germany, Switzerland and even Italy for travellers with time on their hands.

Mark Smith, a former ORR and Department for Transport executive who runs the Man in Seat 61 travel website, reckons ticket prices could drop by close to a third.

“You’d be looking at more capacity, higher service standards and fares that could be 30pc lower based on what we have seen with the advent of competition in Italy and Spain,” he says.

“That will in turn drive further market share gains for rail compared with the airlines and make it feasible to travel further into Europe on a single ticket.”

Customer service front and centre

Virgin has so far been tight-lipped on what the Channel tunnel service might look like, with Phil Whittingham, its project lead, saying only that the route is “ripe for change” and that Sir Richard intended to build a “premium customer experience on board”.

A spokesman adds: “We don’t want to ruin the element of surprise, but just as we’ve done with Virgin Atlantic and our holidays and hotels offering, you can expect bold ideas with the customer experience front and centre.”

On Virgin Atlantic, that experience has included in-flight bar and massages, with a shift to focusing on tech innovation in recent years, including free Wi-Fi from Elon Musk’s Starlink and an AI-powered virtual concierge.

Virgin has specified single-decker trains for its purchase from Alstom, with one insider suggesting that they were more compatible with providing a full at-seat meal service than the double-deckers with which Eurostar is renewing its fleet.

Virgin has said it intends to operate an initial six return trains a day between London and Paris starting in October 2030, later increasing to 13, followed by four to Brussels and three to Amsterdam.

That would represent a substantial increase on the current timetable, with Eurostar offering 14 daily services to Paris, eight or nine to Brussels and five to Amsterdam.

The company, owned by French state railway SNCF, said Virgin’s plan confirmed “the huge potential for growth in international rail” and that it intended to “play a full part in that growth”.

Jon Worth, an expert in European railways, says Virgin had impressed with its work to secure access to St Pancras, the line to the tunnel and the last remaining space at Temple Mills maintenance shed near Stratford before Trenitalia.

“Seeing this project through has been like threading the eye of a needle,” he adds. “Forget the rhetoric from Branson about transforming travel. They’ve been very methodical and very clear headed in devising a project that will just about fit with all these restrictions.”

No room for slippage

However, he says Virgin had taken a risk in choosing a bespoke version of a train built by Alstom in Italy which has not yet been approved in France, introducing the “nightmare” scenario of the trains not being ready for 2030.

Any slippage could open the door to Trenitalia, which is viewed as among the most aggressive of European high-speed operators.

Trenitalia’s train order, from Hitachi Rail, adds to an existing commitment with the Japanese manufacturer and will provide guaranteed delivery times, potentially beating Virgin to the market by a year.

Worth says Trenitalia is likely to expand on routes such as Paris to Lyon and Marseilles and Milan, rather than focusing on London.

Eurostar’s switch to double-deckers for an order of up to 50 new trains may also be problematic, he adds, since the Celestia model is not currently compliant with evacuation requirements within the tunnel in the event of fire.

It is likely that a significant number of the new trains will instead be used on the Paris-Brussels route that Eurostar took over in 2022, easing the pressure on Virgin.

Waiting in the wings are Evolyn, backed by Spanish industrialist Jorge Cosmen, an investor in the owner of National Express, the Dutch startup Heuro, and UK-based Gemini, which has proposed running trains from Stratford and Ebbsfleet to avoid the St Pancras bottleneck.

According to Smith, of the Man in Seat 61 website, Virgin’s best bet will be to play to its strengths by offering upmarket food and wine, exploring initiatives such as allowing carriage of bicycles and dogs, which is currently banned from most Eurostar services.

He says: “It’s that hard-to-define Virgin pizazz that people most want to see and they’ll need to bring that to these trains.”

data.title: Lime withdraws bikes from London borough after complaints from blind residents
data.description:
Lime has removed its electric bikes from a London borough after the company’s vehicles were accused of endangering blind residents.

The company said it had stopped users from being able to hire e-bikes in Bromley, south-east London, where it was operating without an agreement.

It came after Jason Beal, a resident, said he had had to force his guide dog into a busy road because of the company’s lime green bikes being strewn over the pavement.

Councillors had also threatened to pull Lime’s bikes off the streets and charge the company for the hassle.

Liam Conlon, the area’s MP, raised the matter with Bromley council after Mr Beal contacted him to complain.

Lime’s e-bikes have become ubiquitous in London and a popular way of getting around, but the hundreds of them parked on pavements have been seen by critics as a nuisance.

The company had started offering e-bike hire in the Bromley suburb of Penge in recent weeks, despite not having local approval. 

Lime put this down to a technical issue in which the map for neighbouring Lewisham mistakenly covered parts of Bromley. Councillors said they had “blighted” local areas and caused hazards on pavements.

Simon Fawthrop, of Bromley council, said: “We have already raised concerns with Lime that they appear to be operating without our consent in part of our borough.

“Bromley council have long had misgivings about Lime Bikes and other similar bikes that are quite frankly blighting some areas, where they are strewn across pavements causing multiple hazards.

“The council has not agreed anything with Lime and we call upon them to remove their bikes from our borough forthwith.”

Mr Beal, 53, told the London Standard that bikes parked on the pavement meant he had to walk on the road and listen out for traffic, frightening Caine, his guide dog.

“There have been a number of times the Lime bikes have been parked up or propped up against the tree or left over the pavement,” he said.

“So I’ve got to make a decision to try to take him into the main road. That’s a very frightening experience for myself.”

Lime was recently valued at $1.7bn (£1.3bn) in a US initial public offering.

The company operates bikes and scooters in more than a dozen London boroughs.

It has been blighted by claims of personal injuries caused by the bikes, and said recently that it had set aside $56m for personal injury claims.

Lime apologised to Mr Beal and said that it had suspended bike hiring in the borough until it could agree an approach “with appropriate parking locations”.

data.title: Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs as Trump’s tariffs take their toll
data.description:
Jaguar Land Rover is to cut 4,000 jobs as it reels from the impact of Donald Trump’s tariffs and a major cyber attack.

The British car manufacturer will carry out the redundancies over the next two years in an effort to save around £1.7bn.

It marks a major escalation of JLR’s cost-cutting efforts after the company said in July it would axe around 300 roles.

The carmaker, which is owned by India’s Tata Motors, employs more than 30,000 people in the UK.

JLR is under pressure to shore up its finances amid rising costs and a slump in sales. Revenues fell by almost 10pc in the first quarter, while pre-tax profits dropped by two thirds to £109m.

The manufacturer, whose largest market is North America, has been rocked by Mr Trump’s 10pc tariff on vehicle imports.

It is also still reeling from a crippling cyber attack that shut down production for more than a month and is estimated to have cost the company £1.9bn.

Supply chain disruption and tough competition from cut-price Chinese rivals have taken a further toll.

The cuts, first reported by the Sunday Times, represent a major setback to Andy Burnham’s pledge to re-industrialise Britain.

JLR’s global headquarters are in Coventry, while it operates major factories in manufacturing sites in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Merseyside.

Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, said there had been a “perfect storm” hanging over the UK’s automotive industry.

She added: “Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments.”

The union boss said she would meet Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, and JLR chief executive PB Balaji next week.

A spokesman for the Government said that “significant action” had been taken to support carmakers, including lowering electricity bills and creating subsidies for the manufacturing and sale of zero-emission vehicles.

It comes after JLR last month delayed the rollout of its all-electric Defender model, which had been expected after a full redesign of the standard model.

The redesign has been paused for two years, meaning the brand’s best-selling off-roader will not go all-electric until the 2030s.

JLR is not the only major car manufacturer rolling out sweeping cuts amid a slowdown in sales and growing competition from China.

Volkswagen this week confirmed plans to cut 50,000 jobs, marking the biggest programme of cost-cutting in the German car giant’s 89-year history.

A JLR spokesman said: “As we deliver the next phase of our strategy we need to adapt to evolving global market conditions while targeting approximately £1.7bn of savings over the next two years and reduce break-evens to 300,000 vehicles. To achieve this, we must further simplify our organisation, improve efficiency, and build greater resilience.

“Today, we informed our colleagues and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business. We will share further information with our colleagues first.”

Fixed-rate bonds are savings accounts that lock away your funds for a set period of time, paying a guaranteed rate of interest throughout this term.

They can be a shrewd move in times when savings rates are on the way down – as they are now – since the rate you fix at will be unaffected until the term ends.

However, you’ll need to be sure you won’t need the cash in the meantime. Many accounts simply won’t let you access your savings until the term is over, while those that do allow early withdrawals will usually deduct your interest as a penalty.

What are fixed-rate bonds?

Fixed-rate bonds may also be referred to as fixed-rate savings accounts, or even fixed-term deposits – depending on the provider. In essence, they are savings accounts that pay a set amount of interest, and last for a set amount of time.

They commonly span from nine months to five years and, in theory, the longer the term you commit to, the higher the interest rate you receive.

However, this is not always the case – during times when rates are expected to fall over the longer term, savings providers will increase rates for shorter-term bonds in a bid to avoid paying over the odds in future.

You will often need to pay in a lump sum at the start of the term, rather than making regular deposits, so these accounts tend to suit those with larger amounts to save.

The interest can be paid annually, quarterly or monthly, depending on your provider. In some cases, interest may only be paid at the end of the term – if you have a large amount saved over a number of years, receiving all the interest in one go could mean you will exceed your personal savings allowance and have to pay tax on your returns.

Expert opinion: Things to consider when choosing a fixed-rate bond

  • How long can you afford to lock your money away?
  • How often do you want interest to be paid?
  • Are you earning a competitive rate?
  • Are you in danger of exceeding the personal savings allowance?

Rachel Springall, of the analyst Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, said: “Picking the right fixed bond term entirely depends on someone’s circumstances and how soon they wish to access their pot. There are bonds with fixed terms of just a few months, so these might be useful for someone who has a big lump sum but may need to use it before the year is over, such as a deposit for a home.

“There are fixed bonds available that pay interest monthly, which may be suited to customers looking to supplement their income.”

She also warned savers to consider the personal savings allowance (PSA) when it came to accounts that were not Isas, as there could be tax to pay on the interest you earn.

Fixed-rate bonds are worth considering by anyone who wants certainty in their returns – this can be particularly handy in times of volatility.

While it may be tempting to stick to the high street brands you’re familiar with, it’s not always the route to the best accounts.

“As it stands, some of the top rates available are from challenger banks, which should not be overlooked,” Ms Springall added.

Premium Bonds vs fixed-rate bonds

While Premium Bonds and fixed-rate bonds might sound similar, they are very different:

  • Premium Bonds are only provided by National Savings & Investments (NS&I), while fixed-rate bonds are offered by a number of savings providers.
  • Premium Bonds aren’t savings accounts; you don’t get paid interest. Instead, each £1 bond is entered into a monthly prize draw, where you could win between £25-£1m. Fixed-rate bonds pay a set amount of interest for the duration of the term.
  • Premium Bonds prizes are paid tax-free; savings interest from fixed-rate bonds is taxable unless it’s a fixed-rate cash Isa.

Fixed-rate bond FAQS

You might have to pay tax on the interest your fixed-rate bond earns if it exceeds your tax-free allowance, unlike the money stored in an Isa.

This allowance depends on your tax bracket; basic-rate taxpayers can earn £1,000 in interest tax-free but the limit is £500 for higher-rate taxpayers and no personal savings allowance for additional-rate taxpayers.

Those with incomes of less than £17,570 may be able to benefit from the additional starting rate for savings, which gives those on lower incomes up to £5,000 as an extra tax-free savings allowance.

If you usually pay tax by self-assessment, you will be asked to detail the amount of savings interest you have earned over the tax year. If you pay tax via Pay As You Earn (PAYE), any tax on savings interest is usually calculated automatically and your tax code may be adjusted if you have tax to pay.

You must submit a tax return if you earn more than £10,000 in savings interest – regardless of whether or not you usually file one.

This will depend on what rates are available at the time you are looking for a bond, as well as whether the account suits your circumstances.

The best way to determine how “good” an interest rate is, is to see how it compares with other similar types of bond on the market. If it can easily be beaten by other providers, it might be worth looking elsewhere.

They do not pay any interest, instead every £1 you have invested is assigned its own Premium Bonds number, which is entered into a monthly prize draw, whether you could win between £25 and £1m. Our guide to Premium Bonds explains how they work in more detail.

NS&I does offer fixed-rate bonds, including Guaranteed Growth Bonds and Guaranteed Income Bonds – see our guide to NS&I savings accounts to find out more.

Regular savings accounts are set up on the basis that you’ll be contributing little and often. Some may even require you to commit to paying in a certain amount of money each month – commonly between £10 and £500.

Not only are these accounts good for getting into the habit of saving, but you’ll usually be given a higher interest rate for your efforts.

Expert opinion: What restrictions do regular savings accounts have?

There are a few things you should look out for when choosing a regular savings account:

  • High headline interest rates: These can look good initially, but given the restrictions on how much you can deposit you may only earn a relatively small amount of interest overall.
  • Restrictive deposits: You might not be able to save as much as you’d like.
  • Requirements to save every month: Missed deposits may mean you’ll lose out on interest.
  • Withdrawal restrictions: Your money may be locked up for a specified term.

Mark Hicks, of investment and savings platform Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “Regular savers can have a very catchy headline rate. But quite often, the maximum amount of money you can deposit is low. Banks may attract you in with a high interest rate and then you realise you can only save £5,000.”

However, if they can be beneficial if you want to get into the savings habit. “They are very good if you want to deposit small amounts of money and if you’re new to saving,” he added.

Caitlyn Eastell, of Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, agreed: “Regular savings accounts are an ideal choice for those wanting to receive a higher rate of interest or wish to develop and maintain a regular savings habit.

“However, many regular savings accounts don’t give much flexibility on the amount that can be deposited each month and often have minimum or maximum monthly payments.”

Are regular savings accounts worth it?

This really depends on the kind of saver you are, and what you want from an account. Regular savings accounts can be useful if you think you can reliably put away some money every month – which you might not be able to access until the account matures.

If this suits you, you can earn a relatively high rate of interest on what you save, and you’ll hopefully end up with a healthy sum if you stick to your savings habit.

On the other hand, depending on your disposable income, some might find the amounts you’re allowed to save restrictive – and they’re also no good if you’re looking for a home for a lump sum.

What’s more, while the headline interest rates might sound high, you might be surprised to see the interest you earn amounting to fairly little, as deposit restrictions will keep your balance low.

What’s the difference between a savings account and a regular savings account?

A regular savings account is a specific type of savings account.

While some people may think it refers to a “normal” savings account, the “regular” part of its name actually refers to the requirement to save into it regularly.

As mentioned above, the terms will vary and it’s important to make sure you know what you’re signing up to – some providers will reduce the interest paid if you don’t make a deposit every month, while others allow you to save on a more casual basis.

Regular savings FAQs

Yes, you can open more than one account – though some providers might have their own restrictions. Regular savers are for making smaller payments, so there is nothing stopping you from opening several to earn more interest on your money.

Some accounts will have a minimum number of payments you need to make each year – often 10 or 11. Some will require you to pay in a certain amount every month.

Yes, money held in regular savings accounts is protected as long as your account is with a UK-regulated bank or building society, the money is protected under the Financial Services Compensation Scheme up to £120,000 per institution.

Yes, you can open a regular savings account for your children. Check our guide to the best children’s savings accounts to see the latest rates.

A regular savings account can help develop good saving habits. If you are only able to put a small amount of money away each month and would prefer a short-term arrangement, then it might be the best situation for you.

Pros:

  • These accounts can help you get into the savings habit, which can benefit you for the rest of your life.
  • A regular savings account gives you considerably better interest rates than standard accounts, rewarding you for making frequent savings over a year or so.
  • They are inclusive – you’re usually limited to saving relatively small amounts, so those with less to save can still benefit.

Cons:

  • There are generally rigid terms and conditions. The amount you can save is often capped and your interest rate might be reduced if you don’t save every month or if you need to make a withdrawal. Many accounts don’t allow early withdrawals whatsoever.
  • You usually need to have another product with the same bank – usually a current account.
  • The rate sometimes lasts for a limited time, often a year, meaning your money is moved to an account with lower interest rates at the end of the term.
  • Some accounts have variable interest rates – meaning the provider can change the rates whenever they want – so it’s important to keep an eye on messages from the provider and switch, if the rates drop too low.

data.title: Meccano relaunched in attempt to become ‘Britain’s Lego’
data.description:
It was high on the Christmas wish list of millions of British children growing up in the 1960s and 1970s.

But in recent years, Meccano, the classic construction kit made up of metal strips and plates held together by nuts and bolts, has almost disappeared to toy heaven in the computer-game era.

The venerable 125-year-old brand is being dusted down and revived for a new generation with the aspiration to create a “British Lego”.

Meccano’s new British rights owner, The Entertainer, believes it is a “sleeping giant” that can recover from its commercial near-death experience to once again take its place on the world stage.

Andrew Murphy, the chief executive of Teal Group, The Entertainer’s parent company, said: “From a consumer perspective in the UK, Meccano has barely existed for 10 years.

“There may have been some dusty boxes on shelves somewhere but as a major consumer product in the UK it just wasn’t there.”

Global sales dwindled to just £7m under the ownership of the Canadian giant Spin Master, the world’s fourth-biggest toy company, which bought Meccano in 2018.

But the Toronto-based multinational signed a long-term licensing agreement with Teal in January 2025 in an effort to reverse its fortunes.

Mr Murphy said he was convinced the brand has the potential to grow sales “easily into the hundreds of millions of pounds” by tapping into a renewed interest in engineering.

The chief executive added: “We get people all the time asking for something that’s ‘like Lego but not Lego’. That is the role Meccano has played in the past and can again.”

Meccano’s relaunch will be marked by the release of two new limited-edition collective sets: Meccano Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Race Car, with 1,203 pieces and priced at £200, and a Meccano Ducati Monster Motorbike priced at £40.

There will also be four new product ranges: Makers, Builders, Masters and Pro for different age groups starting from three-plus.

Packaging and the once notoriously complex building instructions have been overhauled for a modern audience.

data.title: Sale of Barclay family’s former retail empire to be shelved
data.description:
An auction of the retail empire formerly owned by the Barclay family is set to be shelved after bidders failed to meet the £2bn asking price.

Very Group, the online retailer that also owns the Littlewoods brand, was bought by US private equity firm Carlyle for a nominal £1 sum last year and subsequently put up for sale.

But plans to sell the company now appear to be in jeopardy after none of the potential suitors, which included Chinese online giant JD.com, came up with offers large enough to meet Carlyle’s demands, Sky News reported.

Carlyle, which had been Very’s main creditor, seized control of Very in November following the collapse of the Barclay empire amid a dispute with Lloyds Banking Group about unpaid debts.

In addition to JD.com, possible bidders are said to have included investment firm Elliott, which owns Waterstones, and plus-size online retailer N Brown, which owns the Jacamo and Simply Be brands.

Should Carlyle decide to scrap the sale, it would be left owning the struggling retailer indefinitely.

The Barclay family had owned Very Group for more than two decades as part of a sprawling business empire which once included The Telegraph and London’s Ritz hotel.

Liverpool-based Very Group was created in 2005 through the merger of Littlewoods and Shop Direct.

But the company, which has more than four million customers and delivers more than 40 million items annually, has fallen on hard times in recent years.

Very’s latest full accounts show it made a pre-tax loss of more than £500m on sales of around £2.1bn in the last financial year.

But the most recent trading update for the 39 weeks to March 28 revealed a more upbeat picture with operating profit before exceptional items steady at £173.5m, amid a return to top-line growth.

The group said revenue for the year to date was up 0.3pc to £1.6bn despite “ongoing challenges in the market”. Full-year profits are expected to reach between £310m and £320m.

Carlyle pumped £150m into Very Group earlier this year to help keep it afloat and is seeking to recover that and its earlier loans alongside fellow creditor International Media Investments, the Abu Dhabi media vehicle that backed a failed bid to buy The Telegraph from the Barclay family.

The Barclay family launched an aborted effort to sell Very last year before ultimately ceding control to Carlyle, marking the end of their involvement in the company after two decades.

Sources close to Very Group described it as “a strong, high-quality business [with a] highly resilient trading performance, improved profitability and continued strength with its integrated retail and financial services model, despite ongoing challenges in the market”.

Very Group declined to comment.

Regardless of why you’re saving – for a house, a holiday, your children’s future or as a buffer to cover emergencies – you’ll want to make sure your money is working as hard as possible.

In this article, we will cover:

  • The best fixed-rate bonds

Why do rates matter?

Seeking out an account with a more competitive interest rate can make a huge difference.

For example, take a savings account paying a relatively low 0.75pc. A saver with £50,000 in this account will earn around £375 a year in interest. Moving the deposit to an account with a better rate can mean a difference of thousands. Take an account at the higher end offering 4.75pc – you’d yield £2,427 a year, an extra £2,052.

Cash loses value over time if it is left in an account that pays less than the inflation rate. At the current inflation rate of 2.9pc, a pot of £1,000 left in a zero-interest account would be worth just £971.82 after a year in real terms, and just £866.81 after five years. Our inflation calculator can show how your savings are affected.

What is a savings account?

Unlike a current account, which you’ll use to pay your bills and for everyday spending, a savings account is designed to be the place where you can stash your spare money away, where it will hopefully grow over time.

There are several different types of savings accounts – some offer variable rates, which can change at any time, while some require you to commit to locking your cash away for a fixed period.

In theory, the more inconvenient an account is, the more interest you should earn – but it’s not always the case.

The best fixed-rate bonds for 2026

The best variable savings account rates for 2026

Variable-rate accounts tend to come with more flexibility than fixed-rate deals; often, you can make as many withdrawals as you like without taking a hit on interest, but some specific deals have their own restrictions.

In general, easy-access accounts let you take out money whenever you like; regular saver accounts require you to make deposits regularly; while notice accounts allow you to make withdrawals, but only if you give your provider a prescribed amount of notice.

By clicking through to each of our guides you can find out today’s best rates.

Regular savings account

In some cases, current accounts will pay interest on the balance of money they hold, which can be useful if you don’t want the hassle of transferring money between multiple accounts.

The best Isa rates for 2026

Cash Isas work in a similar way to savings accounts, except that all interest you earn is tax-free – and you’re restricted to depositing up to £20,000 in each tax year. Income tax is payable on savings interest earned outside of an Isa, above an allowance of £1,000 for a basic-rate taxpayer and £500 in the higher-rate band.

Lifetime Isa

Savers who are under 40 and putting money away to buy a home or fund their retirement can open a Lifetime Isa. As well as the tax-free savings growth, the Government rewards savers with a bonus of 25pc, up to £1,000 a year.

The best children’s accounts

If you’re under the age of 18, or saving on behalf of a youngster, you can open a children’s account. Many account providers will let children add and withdraw money from the age of seven, so it can be a good way to teach financial skills early in life.

Children also get their own Isa allowance of £9,000 a year, which means an adult saving on behalf of a child in a Junior Isa can put this extra amount away on top of their own £20,000 allowance.

What is happening to savings rates?

Hundreds of savings accounts currently offer a rate that beats CPI inflation, which measured 2.9pc in July, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics.

Savings rates have risen slightly in recent months, as the economic impacts of war in Iran reversed expectations for further Bank Rate cuts this year. However, should inflation also rise as a result, savings rates may still be unable to keep up.

The most competitive rates can be quick to disappear – so if you spot an account that looks good, you may need to act fast.

Alice Haine, head of personal finance at Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “For now, the best savings rates are continuing to outstrip inflation, giving savers who hunted out the top deals a healthy real return on their nest eggs. Locking in a top rate now before the best deals disappear could be a sensible strategy for those with cash languishing in an account delivering dismal returns to ensure their money is working as hard as possible.”

Use our calculator to see how much your savings account is earning you – and how much more interest you could get if you switched.

What is the difference between an Isa, bond, savings and a current account?

A current account is a transactional account that typically pays no interest but gives you a lot of flexibility in how often you access your money.

With a savings account, the bank pays you interest for keeping your money and therefore imposes some restrictions on how many withdrawals you can make.

A fixed-rate bond is a savings account with a fixed term, usually between one and five years. Until the duration of the bond is up, you cannot withdraw your funds, but in exchange for the commitment you will typically benefit from a higher rate.

The difference between an Isa and other types of savings account is that there is no tax charged on the interest. Everyone can save up to £20,000 a year tax-free in an Isa, or £9,000 for children.

How to choose the right account for you

The first thing to consider is whether you might need access to the funds in an emergency. A current account or an easy-access savings account will give you this flexibility.

However, you will get a higher rate if you are willing to lock away your funds for a set period (for example, in a bond). Generally, the longer the period, the higher the rate – however, this is not the case at the moment. Fixed-rate accounts with one and two-year terms are far higher than those with five-year rates.

The other thing to consider is whether you are at risk of exceeding your personal savings allowance. This is £1,000 for a basic-rate taxpayer and £500 for a higher-rate taxpayer. If you earn more than this in interest outside of an Isa, then you will have to pay income tax.
