data.title: Save over £10,000 with our September money makeover
data.description:
Receive free, personalised tips on how to improve your financial situation. Here’s how to apply* or fill in the form below.

September is a month of fresh starts; a new season, a new school year and a chance to give yourself a new start for the final months of the year. It’s also an ideal time to give your finances a check-up.

You may well be suffering from a summer spending hangover after trips away and days out. Meanwhile, the threat of needing to put the heating on is looming and Christmas spending is on the horizon.

With that in mind, now is the time to make some changes that could leave you better off. From hunting down better savings rates and cutting unnecessary costs to checking your mortgage rate and switching household bills, acting now could save you hundreds, if not thousands, of pounds.

Sort out your savings

Keeping on top of your savings is one of the easiest ways to make money with very little effort. If you haven’t checked your interest rate for a while, or switched your account for years, it’s likely you could be earning far more.

Providers commonly drop rates on old accounts over time, reserving market-leading offers for those who are willing to shop around and switch to the latest issues.

If you have a significant amount saved, a quick check on the latest rates – from our best buy savings pages, for example – could mean you’ll earn thousands more in interest over the course of a year.

For example, say you had a savings account paying a relatively low rate of 0.75pc on a balance of £50,000. Each year, you’d earn around £375 in interest. Move that to a top-rate account paying 5pc and you’d earn £2,558 a year, netting you an extra £2,183.

For those without the time or inclination to move savings around on a regular basis, savings platforms such as Raisin UK and Aviva Save are designed to do the hard work for you. Once you’ve signed up, you can access a range of providers under one roof, allowing you to move your money to a better-paying account without going through another application process.

The trade-off is that these platforms only work with a selected number of banks and building societies, so you may not have access to the very best rates available.

Saving: £2,183 a year

Check your mortgage

Mortgage rates have fluctuated in recent months, with some experts warning they’re about to get more expensive because of rapidly rising swap rates. Therefore, it’s a good time to look for a better deal if yours is coming to an end.

Mark Harris, of mortgage broker SPF Private Clients, said: “The mortgage is most people’s biggest outgoing, so ensuring you aren’t paying more than you need to can make a real difference to the overall state of your finances.

“The key thing to remember is to remortgage when you come to the end of your mortgage deal. Ideally, you should start thinking about this a few months before your deal expires.”

Many lenders allow you to lock in a new rate around three to six months before your current one ends. Doing this can prevent you from being rolled on to your lender’s standard variable rate (SVR). These rates are typically uncompetitive, so staying on the SVR could mean paying considerably more each month.

Say you had a 60pc loan-to-value repayment mortgage with a 20-year term. The difference in the interest you’ll pay could be significant. Mr Harris said: “With the average SVR sitting at 7.13pc [according to Moneyfacts, July 2026], on a £150,000 mortgage, this would result in a monthly payment of £1,175.

“But if you remortgaged to a five-year fix with Santander, pegged at 4.66pc, your monthly payments would reduce to £962, saving you £213 per month. Over the five years, this would save you £12,780.”

Saving: £2,556 a year

Switch your bills

September is the perfect time to give your household bills a once-over – particularly your energy, broadband and mobile phone contracts – to see whether savings could be made.

If you’re locked into a fixed-rate energy deal, or a broadband or mobile phone contract, you won’t usually be able to get out of it early without paying a penalty fee. But if you’re on a standard variable energy tariff, or your broadband and mobile phone contracts have ended, you could be in a good position to switch to a better deal.

This is even more important as energy bills will rise from Oct 1. The energy price cap, which limits what energy providers can charge customers on a “standard variable tariff”, will increase by 4pc. This means a typical household will pay £1,723 a year, up £60 from the current cap covering July to September. It will be the highest level since summer 2023.

Vix Leyton, consumer expert at Thinkmoney, said: “Don’t assume the energy price cap is automatically the cheapest deal available. It limits what suppliers can charge customers on default tariffs, but there may be other tariffs available. Compare your actual unit rates and standing charges with alternatives and check exit fees as carefully as the headline saving.”

Figures from price comparison site MoneySuperMarket show households could save up to £382 a year by switching to a fixed-rate tariff.

Meanwhile, Uswitch says households could save £395 a year by moving to a new broadband deal, and £262 a year by switching from a pay-monthly mobile phone contract to a Sim-only deal.

Saving: £1,039 a year

Review your insurance

By the same token, it’s worth checking when your car or home insurance is up for renewal and getting ready to look for a better deal before then.

Simply accepting your renewal quote might seem like the most convenient option, but shopping around could leave you significantly better off. Customers could save up to £485 on their car insurance and up to £210 on home insurance by comparing quotes, according to Compare the Market.

Timing your purchase right can also make a difference. The best time to buy car insurance is 26 days before your renewal date, according to research, with premiums tending to rise the closer you get to your deadline.

Saving: Up to £695 a year

Scrutinise your spending

Next, look for areas where you can trim spending, and then redirect that money into your savings account.

Ms Leyton said: “Go back through at least three months of bank and credit card statements and look for financial drift, like subscriptions that have crept up in price, memberships you barely use, free trials that became paid services and small regular payments you’ve simply stopped noticing.

“Don’t just check your direct debits either, as that is only part of the picture. Look at recurring card payments, PayPal and, crucially, the subscriptions attached to your phone. It’s very easy to sign up for an app, premium feature or free trial through Apple or Google and completely forget it exists.”

It’s also worth remembering that you don’t have to keep paying for a service while you’re not using it. Many, such as streaming subscriptions, can be cancelled and restarted when you need them.

Ms Leyton added: “If you subscribed to Apple TV+ because you wanted to watch Ted Lasso, cancel it when you’ve finished watching it – you don’t have to keep paying until the next season.”

There are plenty of budgeting methods you might want to try to help you keep a handle on your outgoings. The zero-based budgeting method helps you account for every penny, while the 50/30/20 tactic helps you split your income to cover the essentials, nice-to-haves and savings.

Cutting a fairly conservative £50 a month from discretionary spending would leave you £600 better off over a year.

Saving: £600 a year

Check for switching bonuses

Many banks and investment platforms offer incentives for switching, often in the form of cash.

Santander launched a £240 switching offer earlier this week, while you could get £220 for moving to a qualifying HSBC bank account, £200 with NatWest, £175 with Nationwide and First Direct, and up to £200 if you switch to Co-op Bank before Sept 7.

Depending on the terms of the deal, you might need to keep the account open for a certain amount of time, but once that’s done, there’s nothing to stop you from switching elsewhere for another bonus straight afterwards.

Leaving out First Direct, since you can’t use both the HSBC and First Direct switching offers, if you were to cycle through all the other available options, you would gain £1,035.

Moving your investments can also earn you cashback. Until the end of September, you can earn up to £300 cashback for transferring your investments to IG. You’ll need to move £30,000 to get the maximum amount.

It’s well worth looking for these bonuses, particularly if you were thinking of switching providers anyway. But always check qualifying criteria carefully and make sure the account or platform is right for you.

Saving: Up to £1,335

Don’t miss out on extra help

Finally, it pays to make sure you’re claiming everything you’re entitled to. Take advantage of benefits calculators such as those on the Turn2Us and Entitledto websites to help you. For example:

  • You can claim child benefit if you are responsible for a child under 16, or under 20 if they are in full-time education or training. You’ll receive £27.05 a week for the first child and £17.90 per child for additional children. However, if you or your partner earn £60,000 or more, you might need to repay some or all of the benefit via PAYE or a tax return.
  • Attendance allowance can give you up to £114.60 a week if you have a disability or health condition that requires someone else to help look after you. It’s not means-tested.
  • If you care for someone with substantial caring needs and meet the qualifying criteria, carer’s allowance would give you an extra £86.45 a week.
  • If you are the only adult living in your property, the single-person council tax discount gives you 25pc off your bill. With the average council tax bill standing at £2,343, that could save you £585 a year. Alternatively, if you are on a low income or claim certain means-tested benefits, you could be eligible for a discount of up to 100pc of your bill.

Saving: Depends on your eligibility, but claiming child benefit for one child and claiming the single-person discount for council tax would save you £1,991.60 per year.

Total savings: £10,399

data.title: FTSE aerospace supplier sold to US bidder for £1.9bn
data.description:
A 103-year-old UK aerospace supplier is poised to leave the London stock market after being sold to a US private equity firm.

Bodycote, which is one of the world’s leading metallurgy companies, is to be taken over by New York’s Veritas Capital for £1.85bn.

It will see the Macclesfield company enter private hands for the first time in more than half a century, following its initial stock market listing in 1972.

Bodycote’s takeover is one of a trio of deals announced on Tuesday that will reignite concerns about the ailing health of the London stock market.

Gamma Communications, a FTSE 250 telecoms company, separately agreed a £1.1bn sale to Epris, a London private equity firm. Capricorn Energy, a Scottish oil-and-gas company, struck a deal to sell itself to Norway’s oldest oil company, DNO, for £292m.

Bodycote is the world’s biggest provider of specialist metallurgical treatments, spanning a global network of around 135 workshops.

The FTSE 250 company was started as a textiles manufacturer in Leicestershire in 1923 before moving into the metallurgy industry in the 1970s.

The metals it makes are used in everything from Rolls-Royce’s aerospace engines to specialist drills for undersea mines. It has around 4,000 employees.

The takeover will see Bodycote’s shareholders paid 940p per share, marking a 44pc premium on its closing price on July 7, the day before Veritas submitted its initial offer.

James Dimitri, from Veritas, said: “Bodycote has established itself as a global leader in providing essential technologies for performance metallurgy across a range of mission-critical end markets.”

Veritas is an American private equity firm with around $42bn (£36bn) worth of investments.

Since its launch, Veritas has made more than 145 acquisitions of mostly British and American businesses, including Scottish energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie in 2023.

London’s shrinking stock market

The takeover is the latest in a series of acquisitions that have seen some of Britain’s biggest companies pulled off the London Stock Exchange.

Capricorn Energy, which also announced a deal to go private on Tuesday, owns stakes in four oil and gas fields in the Egyptian desert, and is exploring more sites in the area.

DNO, which was started in 1971, is listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange and has oil sites in the Middle East, West Africa and the North Sea.

Berkshire-based Gamma sells phone and internet services to businesses across Western Europe, including the University of Derby and the AA.

Low valuations have made London-listed companies attractive to international buyers. It has fuelled an exodus from the London Stock Exchange, with the number of listed companies falling from 2,365 a decade ago to around 1,500 today.

Most recently, Tate & Lyle was taken over by US rival Ingredion in a £2.7bn deal in June that ended its 90-year stint on London’s main market.

Wise cancelled its listing on the London Stock Exchange in May after shifting its primary listing to New York. Flutter Entertainment, which owns Betfair and Paddy Power, shifted its own listing from London to New York in 2024.

data.title: Developers told to demolish 16ft wall that ruined woman’s sea view
data.description:
Developers have been ordered to demolish a 16ft wall that blocked a woman’s sea view and left her feeling “trapped” inside her own home.

Liz Bates claimed the 16ft-long, 6ft-high brick wall, which was added to a block of 27 luxury apartments without permission, knocked about £50,000 off the value of her home in the Southbourne area of Bournemouth.

The two-storey block in front of her home has an outdoor roof terrace attached to the side of the building, with the wall intended to shield residents from view.

Vivir Estates, the developers, claimed the wall was necessary to prevent “mutual overlooking” between the new apartment and Mrs Bates’s balcony.

They appealed after Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole council rejected a retrospective application they submitted in February.

The appeal has been rejected by the Planning Inspectorate.

David Kay, a planning inspector, said the wall had a “harmful overbearing impact” on Mrs Bates’s home and the size of the roof terrace “far exceeded what could be reasonably described as modest”.

He added that the terrace could be used for large parties that would cause “significant levels of noise and disturbance” to Mrs Bates.

He highlighted the risk of “overheard conversations” and said that while the apartment’s new occupiers would be aware of the “privacy” issues before moving in, Mrs Bates could not have known as she already lived there.

He concluded: “The appeal development would be contrary to the development plan, read as a whole, and that there are no material considerations that would justify determining other than in accordance with it. Therefore, the appeal should be dismissed.”

Mrs Bates said the appeal outcome gave her a “huge sense of relief” and urged the council to carry out enforcement action straight away.

“An appeal decision should mean something. If development continues in breach of planning control, residents need to have confidence that the council will take appropriate enforcement action rather than leaving us to repeatedly monitor the site, raise concerns and respond to retrospective applications,” she said.

“We would ask the council to take a firm approach and use its enforcement powers.

“Residents should not have to become de facto planning enforcement officers simply because work has been carried out without the necessary permission.

“What started as a planning issue has become something that has affected our home life, our sense of privacy and security in our own home, and our overall wellbeing.

“There has been the constant uncertainty of not knowing what will happen next, having to monitor building work and planning applications, prepare objections and spend our own time trying to understand an incredibly complicated planning process.

“It has been exhausting and, at times, overwhelming,” Mrs Bates said.

“Home is supposed to be the place where you can switch off, but for a long time this situation has made it very difficult to do that. The appeal victory has given us some hope that there may finally be light at the end of the tunnel.”

Vivir Estates has been approached for comment on the unsuccessful appeal.

Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole council said: “As this is a live investigation, it would not be appropriate to comment on any potential enforcement action or timescales at this stage.

“Any further action will be considered in accordance with national planning policy and guidance, the relevant statutory framework and the council’s adopted planning enforcement plan.”

data.title: City in row with Historic England over skyscrapers near Tower of London
data.description:
A fresh row has erupted between the City and the Government’s heritage watchdog because of skyscrapers surrounding the Tower of London.

Historic England has called for a “larger uninterrupted gap of clear sky” between the Tower and the buildings to preserve views of the landmark. It also argued that new buildings should “lean away” from the monument.

But the City of London Corporation has warned these proposals would kill one million sq ft of office tower projects.

The dispute pits the financial district’s economic ambitions against conservationist fears that its expansion will threaten the Tower of London’s status as a world heritage site.

The Corporation had prepared to sign off its planning policies for the next 16 years this summer, but Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, intervened amid concerns regarding the plan’s potential effect on the Tower of London.

The proposals will be considered again by planning inspectors this week after Mr Pennycook requested more hearings on the topic.

The City warns that restricting the heights of planned office towers could make it commercially impossible for property developers to build them.

This is because property developers rely heavily on the upper floors, which are the most valuable to rent out to tenants, to make their projects stack up financially.

The City of London Corporation said in a report for an upcoming planning hearing: “[Historic England’s proposal] would – significantly and demonstrably – reduce the ability of the City to meet [its need] for commercial growth, removing important potential floorspace from the most productive part of the City.

“Historic England’s approach removes floorspace at the higher and more valuable parts of the contours.”

The Corporation instead suggested that buildings have a “clearly defined edge” that would leave views unblocked.

United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization raised concerns in July about the effect of high-rises on the fortress’s reputation.

Its world heritage committee has requested a UK visit before February next year to assess its “state of conservation”.

Tom Sleigh, the chairman of the City of London’s planning and transportation committee, said: “The City’s postcodes are the most economically productive in the country.

“To harm their growth without good reason at a time of national economic urgency would be like entering a race with your shoelaces tied together.

“The City has grown alongside the Tower of London for nine centuries; the two have never been a choice ... Business needs a decision and soon.”

A Historic England spokesman said: “We are keen to work together to identify solutions to reduce the potential for further harm to the Tower of London world heritage site whilst still achieving major economic growth.

“Reducing the potential for harm is of vital importance to the conservation of the world heritage site and we believe critical to minimising the potential for the Tower of London to be included on the list of world heritage in danger.”

data.title: Housebuilder warns of £10m loss amid property market slump
data.description:
Shares in Crest Nicholson have slumped to a record low after the struggling housebuilder warned it would post a loss amid a deepening slump in the property market.

Crest said it now expected to post a loss of £10m for the full year, reversing previous guidance of a £5m to £10m profit.

It also said it would build up to 1,400 homes this year, down from an earlier forecast of as many as 1,500. It marks the company’s third cut to guidance in the last six months.

Crest’s shares dropped by as much as 12pc in early trading to a new record low.

Martyn Clark, chief executive of Crest Nicholson, said the business was making “tangible progress” but that trading had “remained difficult over the summer”.

He said: “Although the timing of a broader market recovery remains uncertain, the group is taking the right actions to protect liquidity and improve operational execution, while positioning the business for recovery when market conditions normalise.”

Crest also warned that crunch talks with its lenders were taking longer than expected, months after the company disclosed it was looking for flexibility over the terms of its debt.

The London-listed housebuilder said it remained in “constructive discussions” with its lenders but that it “anticipates some slippage” in its timetable again.

Crest had delayed publishing its results in July in the hopes of reaching an agreement with the banks, but ended up reporting a £35m loss while warning its discussions remained unresolved.

It has sought to shore up its finances by cutting spending and selling extra land, which has helped cut debt by around £30m. Net debt is expected to stand between £70m and £90m at the end of the financial year.

Bosses said market conditions had been “more subdued than expected”, blaming weaker demand and aggressive pricing by rival housebuilders.

Crest’s difficulties will put further pressure on Labour’s ambition to build 1.5 million homes during this parliament.

data.title: John Lewis boss warns Labour against ‘terrible’ high street tax raid
data.description:
The boss of John Lewis has warned John Healey that a Budget tax raid on large stores would have a “terrible impact” on town centres and high streets across the UK.

Peter Ruis, the outgoing managing director of the department store chain, issued a plea to the Chancellor not to raise the business rate multiplier on thousands of shops and supermarkets with a rateable value of more than £500,000.

That includes all 36 of its department stores, many of which serve as “anchors”, attracting shoppers to town and city centres.

Retailers fear that Labour plans to increase business rates on large shops to pay for a cut in the bills for pubs, clubs and live-music venues pledged by Andy Burnham in the first week of his premiership.

Speaking at John Lewis’s flagship Oxford Street store on Thursday, Mr Ruis said it was “really, really critical” that ministers resisted the temptation to do so.

He said: “It would be a terrible impact for all retailers. No one wants those city centres and those town centres and those high streets with closed shops.

“A lot of the smaller stores who won’t be affected by that are also against it because they need people like us.

“John Lewis is the anchor to pretty much everywhere we are, and people drive into that town centre to visit us and then visit everyone else as well, so it’s really, really critical that that doesn’t happen.”

Mr Ruis, who will leave John Lewis at the end of the week, joins a chorus of senior industry figures who have urged the Chancellor not to raise the multiplier when he makes his maiden Budget speech on Oct 28.

Earlier this week, the Retail Jobs Alliance, which represents some of the biggest names in the sector including Asda, Marks & Spencer and Tesco, called for restraint.

In a letter to the Prime Minister, the coalition said: “Retail stores are integral to high street renaissance, but they cannot continue investing in communities if they face an ever-increasing tax burden.”

Rachel Reeves raised the higher multiplier by 2.8p to 50.8p in her final Budget last November. The new business rates regime came into force in April.

Mr Ruis was unveiling a major shake-up of the Oxford Street flagship as part of a £150m investment programme in physical stores.

It includes the rollout of a new upmarket restaurant and bar concept called Platter, as well as tech and wellbeing-focused sports departments.

The Oxford Street branch also opened the chain’s first fine-art outlet after launching a concession of the Clarendon Fine Art gallery group.

Works on sale at the opening included a Damien Hirst priced at £23,500, a David Hockney drawing with a £10,500 price tag and a Picasso lithograph available for £15,950.

The warning from John Lewis came as new figures revealed a 1.7pc decline in footfall in the year to August as shoppers steered clear of the high street.

The British Retail Consortium (BRC) called for action on business rates and energy costs in the Budget, urging Mr Healey to “throw Britain’s high streets a lifeline”.

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “Retail faces cost pressures and households are watching every penny.

“Government action on business rates and energy costs would help keep prices down, support investment and sustain the jobs and communities that retail underpins across the country.”

data.title: Waitrose takes on M&S with £10m investment in posh ready-meals
data.description:
Waitrose is poised to trigger a £10m luxury ready-meal battle with its rival Marks & Spencer as the supermarket seeks to cash in on the eating-in boom.

The John Lewis-owned grocer has created 29 new stick-it-in-the-oven dishes with wagyu beef, 12-month-aged Italian Parmigiano Reggiano cheese and six-hour slow-cooked brisket among the dishes now on its ready-meal menu.

A further 30 existing dishes are also receiving makeovers as squeezed middle-class British consumers increasingly shun restaurants and gastropubs where the bill for a meal for two can easily exceed £100.

The premium ready-meal sector is one of the fastest-growing categories in food retailing, with Waitrose sales surging 11pc last year compared with 8pc for ready-meals as a whole.

However, the luxury dine-at-home market is still dominated by Marks & Spencer, which has had significant success with its Gastropub range and its tie-in with Tom Kerridge, the celebrity chef. It claims to have a 47pc share of the dine-in category.

Waitrose bosses are hoping to grab some of that share with its newly expanded No 1 range, dominated by Asian and Italian recipes.

The supermarket is investing £10m in three years to research and design dishes that it hopes will appeal to shoppers used to dining out several times a week but now questioning the cost.

‘Spending has definitely shifted’

The investment in upmarket meals comes as Waitrose’s sister company, the John Lewis department store group, faces “really tough trading” according to Jason Tarry, the partnership’s chairman.

Waitrose says it is using “traditional cooking methods” and “authentic ingredients” to create the meals, which will go on sale on Wednesday.

The new range includes six-hour slow-cooked beef and chianti pappardelle, Calabrian nduja and sausage ragu orecchiette with mascarpone, Kerala-inspired fish curry, miso aubergine, wagyu cottage pie and butternut and mascarpone bucatini.

Mains are priced at between £6 and £7.50 while sides, such as slow-cooked black dal and coconut rice, cost between £3.60 and £5.30. There is also an £18 meal deal for two mains and two sides.

Analysts said the cost of living squeeze, soaring restaurant bills and fears of higher interest rates after the surge in energy prices were all driving the growth of the luxury ready-meal sales.

Nicholas Found, the head of commercial content at analysts Retail Economics, said: “Spending has definitely shifted from restaurant to at home meals. Retailers are providing much improved quality, and the gap between what you buy in store and some of the eating out options has narrowed markedly in recent years.

“The anxiety about inflation and the potential for interest rates to go up is there, but consumer do not want to compromise on their treats. The dine-in option really plays into that.”

The race to create ever-more-sophisticated dine-at-home options has brought the ready-meal a long way from its frozen TV dinner and boil-in-a-bag origins.

Marks & Spencer is credited with launching the first ready-meal recognisable to modern UK consumers in 1979 with its chicken kiev.

It is now also upgrading its dine-in range with new lines, such as aubergine parmigiana and mozzarella, and hot honey ravioli. Recipes are also being overhauled with all pasta now made with 100pc olive oil instead of seed oil.

The UK ready-meal market is estimated now to be worth £5.4bn annually, rising to £13.7bn by 2034, according to analysts Market Data Forecasts.

The UK is by far the biggest market in Europe, accounting for almost a third of total spending. Waitrose research shows that around half its customers buy a ready-meal through the course of a year.

Charlotte Di Cello, at Waitrose, said: “This investment is a step-change in our fresh ready-meals, with authentic ingredients and cooking methods, new recipes and the flavours that make dinner at home feel special.”

Kathryn Turner, at M&S, said: “Customers come to us for restaurant quality food they can enjoy at home without compromising on quality, flavour or value.”

data.title: Dutch shift gold from US to UK because of ‘geopolitical unrest’
data.description:
The Netherlands has moved its gold from the US to Britain because of “increasing geopolitical unrest”.

The Dutch central bank has relocated 86 tonnes of the precious metal to the Bank of England, mostly from New York, as part of its process of “strengthening its crisis preparedness”.

De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB), the country’s central bank, said better distribution of the gold would make it easier to trade and spread risks, and would make it more readily available to use in a crisis.

DNB made no mention of what kind of crisis it was preparing for. However, fears that Donald Trump could impose a tariff on gold previously triggered a scramble to move it out of the US.

Future prices in New York rose to a premium of more than $100 (£74) compared to London as banks, refiners and dealers raced to secure metal for delivery.

Mr Trump eventually clarified that gold would be exempt from tariffs. However, analysts warned that the episode might undermine New York’s position as the largest gold-futures market.

Bullion has historically been exempt from any tariffs because of its important role in the financial system.

“With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves. We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” Olaf Sleijpen, the governor of the DNB, said.

The Netherlands held 612.4 tonnes of gold by the end of 2025, worth €72.2bn (£61.9bn). The bank relocated a portion of the reserves between March and August this year.

“In view of increasing geopolitical unrest, DNB is strengthening its crisis preparedness. Improving the liquidity and tradability of the Dutch gold reserves is part of these preparations,” the bank said in a statement.

The UK operates one of the world’s most important gold markets and the Bank of England’s underground vaults hold the second-largest haul of gold in the world.

A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that 57pc of responding central banks stored some gold at the Bank of England, making it the most widely used foreign custodian.

This includes Venezuela, whose gold has been kept in the UK despite requests from Nicolás Maduro’s government to repatriate it.

At the time of his ousting earlier this year, a lack of formal recognition of Venezuela’s new administration meant that the Bank of England declined to release the gold – then worth more than $3bn.

Maduro, the former Venezuelan president, attempted to retake the gold stored at the Bank in 2018 to prop up his nation’s collapsing economy. However, the Bank refused the request because the UK did not recognise him as Venezuela’s legitimate president.

The Maduro government sued for the return of the precious metal in 2020, but ultimately lost the case in the Supreme Court in 2023.

data.title: Sewage dumped into rivers as rain overwhelms water system
data.description:
Water companies are pumping sewage into rivers as ageing wastewater systems struggle to cope with the return of rain.

Campaign group River Action said there had been 4,600 sewage spill incidents across England and Scotland in the past 48 hours as storm overflows were overwhelmed.

Sewage has been flowing into the River Derwent in Derbyshire for 15 hours, while a spill into the River Windrush in Oxfordshire has been ongoing for 13 hours.

In the UK, a sewage spill is considered legal if it happens during exceptionally heavy rain and only if the sewage is discharged through an outlet named in the water company’s permit.

The incidents in recent days follow the return of rain after weeks of drought, with thunderstorms forecast across England during the bank holiday weekend.

However, Feargal Sharkey, the musician-turned-rivers campaigner, said the level of sewage seeping into the country’s rivers reflected the poor state of Britain’s water system rather than the weather.

Mr Sharkey said: “When there’s the merest hint of rain, copious amounts of sewage are dumped into our rivers and into the water around our beaches. Yet again the profiteering and failure of our water companies to invest is exposed.”

Thames Water spilt effluent into rivers for more than 100,000 hours in 2025, despite it being a dry year.

Severn Trent Water was the only water company to receive a top rating for its environmental performance last year, but nonetheless recorded more than 30,000 spillage incidents.

Utility companies are in the middle of an investment programme meant to reduce sewage spills. Water UK, which represents Britain’s water companies, said the industry was “tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works”.

However, Mark Lloyd, the chief executive of River Action UK, said the investment was too little, too late.

“It is disgraceful that funding for new infrastructure to prevent sewage overflows – and for maintenance of existing assets – was restricted over the past 20 years,” he said.

Mr Lloyd added that the recent spillages were particularly bad, as the preceding drought meant the sewage was potentially more environmentally damaging.

He told The Telegraph: “Sewage overflows after long dry periods can be particularly damaging because there can be accumulations of concentrated sewage in the network that get flushed out into rivers that have low flows and oxygen levels, greatly increasing the impact on fish, invertebrates and other wildlife.”

Andy Burnham has pledged to assert greater control of water companies, saying this month that he was “angry” about the industry’s performance, including on pollution.

data.title: ‘Our English heritage is in peril’: The parish churches facing extinction
data.description:
Should you pass through the village of Marksbury, perched at the junction of the A368 and the A39 between Bath and Bristol, it is unlikely you’d stop to look round the church of St Peter. Hanging back from the traffic, and surrounded by a modest graveyard, it appears almost painfully ordinary save for four awkwardly large 18th-century pinnacles jutting from the tower.

Inside the church there are splatters of mould on the walls. A flat, white ceiling, probably added during the 1950s, gives the medieval nave, which boasts a Norman font, a functional feel. A war memorial pays tribute to four village men killed in the Second World War, each a former member of the church’s Sunday school. Today, the only evidence a thriving Sunday school once existed in St Peter’s is a forlorn smattering of children’s Bible stories.

Like hundreds of parish churches up and down the country, St Peter’s is facing the end of the road. Years of financial pressure, including a major project to stabilise the tower, have eaten up its reserves. It now hosts only two services a month, meaning its tiny, seven-strong congregation – average age around the mid-seventies – must travel to a neighbouring church. In the face of seemingly terminal decline, the Diocese of Bath and Wells decided around 18 months ago to decommission St Peter’s in preparation for sale, with a view to it being converted into a private house. For one member of the congregation, let’s call her Susan, this might mean having to pass through someone else’s garden to visit her husband’s grave.

Who cares, you might think. Almost every village in Britain has a church like St Peter’s – many of them medieval, often with 12th-century origins. Does it matter if the odd unremarkable specimen, gathering dust and damp in the silence, unused by the overwhelming majority of the local community, is turned into a much-needed home?

Well, yes, it does, says Rachel Morley, the indefatigable director of Friends of Friendless Churches (FOFC), which has been rescuing unloved churches from the clutches of decommissioning since 1957. Morley – who is also the author of a glorious new book called Church Crawling, about the hidden histories of English churches – has been director since 2018 and, under her watch, the charity has saved 27, restoring pre-modern beauties, Arts and Crafts gems, peerless Victorian windows and, in some instances, discovering treasures that had lain out of sight for centuries.

“At St Peter’s Church in Wickham Bishops [which was in such a bad state it took FOFC decades to restore], we found four schemes of pre-Reformation wall paintings that nobody knew were there,” she says. That church – a lovely little building consisting of just a nave and a chancel – now has a new lease of life as the studio for a stained-glass window artist.

St Peter’s in Marksbury, whose ownership is in the process of being transferred from the Diocese of Bath and Wells to the FOFC, and which is Grade II* listed, may not have similar treasures to reveal – although one can fantasise about what medieval wonders might have once existed behind the ugly post-war ceiling. Yet for Morley, restoring architectural glory isn’t always the point. Rather, the FOFC preserves decaying places of worship as much in order to retain their unique hallowed grace, or what the Victorian polymath John Ruskin described as their “deep sense of voicefulness, of stern watching, of mysterious sympathy”.

“It’s easy to say a church is unviable because of declining numbers and no clergy, but it’s not just a numbers game,” she says. “Churches offer something special beyond this for future generations to experience as they wish. They are a crucial part of England’s culture.”

The history of conservation in Britain is a story of passionate individuals rather than – as one might be forgiven for expecting – organised political will. The Victorians were zealous restorers, but their enthusiastic interventions often erased a building’s palimpsestic architectural history, prompting Ruskin to argue for the value of protecting old buildings from the outset rather than forcing crass, all-out redevelopment.

In a similar spirit, William Morris, the textile designer and influential thinker, founded the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings in 1877. Ivor Bulmer-Thomas, who founded the FOFC, was a journalist and politician who campaigned tirelessly for the preservation of historic churches. The former poet laureate John Betjeman – another founding member of the Friends of Friendless Churches, along with fellow poet T S Eliot – did much to raise public awareness of the ineffable value of religious buildings. “We accept the collapse of the fabrics of our old churches, the thieving of lead and objects from them,” he harrumphed, “[...] because we are convinced we must save money.”

Yet today the scale of the problem is almost overwhelming. Around 3,500 places of worship have closed in the last decade. Another 1,000 are on Historic England’s At Risk register. A recent Church of England report revealed a £1bn backlog of repairs. The issue has been considerably worsened by Labour’s decision to replace the Listed Places of Worship Grant Scheme – a 25-year-old “lifeline” that allowed churches to reclaim VAT on renovation work and was worth around £42m a year – with the Places of Worship Renewal Fund, worth just over £23m a year for four years and only available in England. (Scotland has a separate fund, but there is no equivalent government support for churches in Wales and Northern Ireland.) The loss of VAT relief has left many churches unable to afford even basic repairs. Morley points out that the £350,000 she expects the FOFC to pay in VAT this year could have saved another condemned church.

Moreover, the new fund is competitive, prioritising “areas of England with the greatest need of investment and those that bring most community benefit”. To Morley, the wording suggests the Government isn’t interested in preserving the fabric of a church building at all. “To basically say you will fund churches in areas of deprivation begs the question: is this a heritage policy? Or is it, at heart, a social one? It seems clear the Government is concerned only with its growth and housing agenda, and doesn’t care or have pride in the things that make England special and enhance our lives beyond the material.

“They talk about health and heritage, or climate change and heritage, but never heritage for its own sake. And because they aren’t glamorous, the value of churches can fall through the gaps. But you have to think about the cumulative benefit of them over time, and that’s just not what the Government is interested in.”

A spokesman for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport insisted that the fund would “prioritise heritage faith buildings in areas with the most need, where funding can have the greatest impact” and said an “upfront capital grant scheme [was] the best way to help historic churches to overcome fundraising barriers.”

Nonetheless, the lack of long-term sustainable funding means that some churches are left decaying for decades, so that, by the time money is found, it is nearly too late. FOFC, which survives on a charitable income of around £2m a year from donations, subscriptions and grants, is currently fighting to raise funds for two alarmingly imperilled churches: St Tyfi in Dinefwr, Carmarthenshire, unused since 1961 and in a terrible state but for the efforts of four locals who for years have done what they can; and St Helen’s, Biscathorpe, Lincolnshire, which boasts a complete Victorian interior but is now one of the most endangered Victorian churches in the country.

Morley argues that an annual government pot of £50m – maintained for the long term – would go a long way to keeping more churches open, if not necessarily full. Yet the question remains: why save these churches if only a very few, invariably elderly people, want to worship in them? Why put money, energy and resources into preserving them if they are only to stand, in the large majority of cases, empty and unloved?

“We’ve got a beautiful church on the Llŷn Peninsula in Wales. It’s a tiny little whitewashed box in a field, and it was recently used for the funeral of a local farmer,” says Morley. “Along came this solemn procession of mourners, of ruddy necks over white shirts and black ties, because the church had served generations of farming communities, and so, of course, this was the place where this man would be buried. And that matters.

“That church is so small, it takes up a tiny patch of land. We don’t need to overthink it. And, yes, it costs money to maintain it, but it’s not breaking the bank. Overall, we’re so much richer for it. Even if it is used only three times a year.

“Perhaps because I am Irish I can see so clearly this rich cultural heritage that churches have, and how very lucky England is to have it.”

Morley acknowledges that her arguments are sometimes emotional rather than pragmatic. Abstract ideas about continuity, roots and belonging don’t easily fit on to a spreadsheet or into a government policy document. Yet, as her new book so persuasively argues, churches are much more than medieval walls and a bell tower; they are numinous spaces that contain traces of the lives of the people who once worshipped there over hundreds of years – or, to quote Ruskin again, the “golden stain of time”.

Together, they serve as an extraordinarily rich crucible of English social and spiritual history. And if there are only two or three in the congregation, does that really matter? At St Peter’s, the hope is that the church can be maintained for the occasional future service and to stand as a symbol of local history.

“It is plain, it is simple, it is certainly no historic treasure trove,” ends the three-page, hand-typed visitor booklet that can be found by the front door. “But it is old, it is the centre of our village and, to the Christians who worship here, it is the centre of our lives.”

Church Crawling: The Secret Lives and Hidden Stories of England’s Churches by Rachel Morley (£22, Bodley Head), is out now. Order your copy here

data.title: CrossCountry cancels almost all trains after power cut
data.description:
CrossCountry has cancelled almost all its trains after a power cut at its Birmingham headquarters.

The long-distance rail operator warned of “significant disruption” on Sunday and said that services “across almost all routes will be withdrawn until further notice”.

The Birmingham city centre power cut has disrupted operations at CrossCountry’s main control centre, meaning systems used to manage its trains are unavailable.

The only CrossCountry route still running is between Peterborough and Stansted airport, calling at March, Ely and Cambridge.

CrossCountry tickets are being accepted via any reasonable route on all other train companies’ services, according to National Rail Enquiries. A normal service is expected to run on Monday.

A spokesman for CrossCountry said: “A power cut in Birmingham city centre has affected the building where our control centre is located. As a result, many of the systems our control teams use to manage the railway are currently unavailable.

“Although colleagues are working hard to safely operate services using alternative processes, CrossCountry services will be significantly disrupted on Sunday Aug 23.

“While we will run as many trains as possible, passengers should expect significant reductions to services and cancellations across almost all routes throughout the day. We are sorry to passengers affected by this significant and unforeseen disruption.

The National Grid operates the electricity distribution network serving Birmingham city centre.

On Aug 7, a similar power cut in Manchester caused a power cut at a Network Rail signalling control centre, leading to chaos across the north-west of England as all trains came to a standstill as a safety precaution.

The incident was triggered by a fault at a transformer in Ardwick, which provides energy for Network Rail’s Manchester Rail Operating Centre.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, said: “I am concerned to hear about a power outage affecting CrossCountry rail services, which I know will be very frustrating to passengers.

“I’ve asked publicly owned operators to lay on extra services where possible. We’ve also sent Network Rail power teams who are on-site and working to restore power and systems as soon as possible.”

A National Grid electricity distribution spokesman said on Sunday afternoon: “Our engineers are on site working to repair a fault affecting CrossCountry’s Birmingham control centre.

“We’re working closely with CrossCountry to restore power safely as soon as possible. We understand the frustration caused by disrupted journeys and are sorry for the inconvenience to passengers.”

Travellers delayed by more than half an hour are eligible to claim Delay Repay compensation from the train company via its website.

data.title: Currys’ turnaround king tasked with reviving tired Boots ahead of flotation
data.description:
When Currys announced that Alex Baldock, its chief executive, was stepping down earlier this year, the response from investors was immediate.

Shares in the electronics chain fell sharply – wiping almost 11pc off its valuation – as markets digested the departure of the man widely credited with engineering the company’s quietly successful turnaround.

Now Baldock appears poised for an even bigger challenge, tasked with reviving a 177-year-old brand that has seen better days. On Wednesday, it emerged that the outgoing Currys chief was being lined up to take the reins at Boots.

The company confirmed his appointment on Thursday, setting the stage for Baldock to try to convince investors that the British chemist could be worth as much as £7bn.

Baldock should be well-suited to the role. He has spent the past seven years proving that legacy retailers can still thrive if they modernise quickly enough.

At Currys, that meant slimming down the store estate, cutting costs, boosting online sales and emphasising its “omnichannel” offering of services, repairs, credit and subscriptions.

Adam Tomlinson, a retail analyst at Berenberg, says that when Baldock arrived at Currys in 2018, “the business was in a very tough place”.

“A major focus initially was restructuring the mobile division, which had become a significant drag on the wider group. He completely realigned it in terms of right-sizing both the store base and the cost base, and turned it from being a problem area into a positive contributor.”

Tomlinson says Baldock’s broader strategy has been to transform Currys from a “product-first retailer into an integrated services business”, encouraging customer loyalty through credit offers, delivery and installation, warranties, repairs and trade-ins.

“What is often overlooked is how much focus he placed on staff and colleagues,” he adds. “He has a mantra that customer experience can never exceed colleague experience.”

Baldock will now have to repeat that success at Boots – a brand which is desperately in need of a turnaround.

Since being folded into Walgreens Boots Alliance in 2014, Boots has endured closures, restructurings and repeated attempts to move away from its old-fashioned chemist image.

Its owners have repeatedly signalled that they would be keen to offload the British business. Walgreens launched a sale process for Boots in 2022.

However, it later scrapped the plans after failing to secure a deal at the valuation it wanted in the face of difficult market conditions and rising borrowing costs. Since then, efforts have been focused on honing the chain, including pushing through further store closures and cost reductions.

Speculation over a sell-off of the British arm was revived last year when private equity firm Sycamore Partners swooped to buy Walgreens Boots Alliance in a $10bn (£7.4bn) deal.

Shortly after the deal was completed, Sycamore split Walgreens into five standalone entities – one of which was Boots. It was seen as the first major step towards ultimately returning the British chemist to the UK stock market.

Baldock is believed by many to have been brought on to get Boots over the line for such a London listing – something insiders claim was “always the plan”. Its owners are looking for a valuation as high as £7bn. Still, some remain unconvinced that any listing would be imminent.

A senior retail industry source says his appointment is the same “as with any private equity-owned business”. “The job is to create as much value as possible for the owners,” the source says.

Given the current state of the London market, they say it is more likely that Baldock has simply been brought in to put Boots on a stronger footing. “I don’t think it’s right that he’s been brought in for an IPO.”

They say Boots’ health and beauty division is now “by far the most important part of the business”, reflecting the growing view inside retail that the future of Boots lies less in pharmacy and more in cosmetics, skincare and wellness.

That shift is already visible inside many of Boots’ larger stores, where beauty halls increasingly dominate the shop floor while traditional pharmacy space shrinks.

Boots has revamped more than 100 of its stores and updated beauty halls in more than 180 sites. It argues that this has helped it to record 20 consecutive quarters of market-share growth.

Analysts expect Baldock to continue pushing the business in the same direction because beauty products offer significantly stronger margins than dispensing medicines or selling low-cost healthcare essentials.

Jonathan De Mello, of JDM Retail, says Boots is “looking at devoting more floor space to beauty rather than distress pharmaceutical purchasing. The margins on beauty products are significantly better”.

At the same time, Boots still faces the challenge of balancing investment in physical stores with the need to boost online sales.

For all the investment Boots has poured into flagship stores and digital infrastructure, analysts argue the business still lags behind rivals on both fronts.

“The Advantage Card is strong, but the website still needs work,” says De Mello.

Former executives claim there are also still swathes of its sprawling estate which are in urgent need of investment. Renovating all of these old stores would be painfully expensive.

Clive Black, another retail analyst, agrees the chain’s estate remains uneven despite years of investment.

“There are some flagship stores where they have clearly invested heavily in beauty, but there are also an awful lot of stores around the country that look pretty tired,” says Black.

If Baldock wants to take Boots public – be it later this year or further down the line – he will have to convince investors that Boots can be a growth business rather than simply a reliable cash generator.

Black says he suspects that “Boots may end up being seen more as an income story than a pure growth story”.

Baldock will also inherit questions over Boots’ international operations.

While the retailer’s presence outside the UK may have formed part of the attraction for him personally – having steered Currys for years in both the UK and overseas – analysts suggest some international businesses could ultimately be sold off as management focuses more tightly on the chain’s strongest markets.

De Mello says Boots’ operations in places such as Germany and Mexico are underperforming. He argues the business would be better concentrating on the UK and Ireland, which he describes as the company’s “engine room for growth”.

At Currys, Baldock managed to convince the markets that physical stores still had value in the Amazon era, provided they worked seamlessly alongside a strong online offer. Between 2024 and 2026, he oversaw a tripling in the retailer’s share price.

Just last week, Baldock told The Times that he loved his role at Currys. His next move would have to be “something properly exciting to take me away from Currys”. With Boots, it seems that Baldock has found that. Now, he said, marked the start of “an exciting new chapter for Boots”.

data.title: Netflix subscription rises above £20 a month for first time
data.description:
Netflix has increased the price of its premium subscription package to above £20 for the first time.

The streaming giant this week quietly lifted the cost of a premium membership by £2 to £20.99 for UK subscribers.

A standard plan has risen by £1 to £13.99, while the cheapest ad-supported tier is now £7.99 – up by more than a third from £5.99.

Netflix said the price rises “reflect improvements to our wide range of entertainment and the quality of our service”.

The premium membership is Netflix’s most expensive package, allowing simultaneous streams on four devices, as well as 4K streaming. When introduced in 2015, the tier cost £8.99 a month.

A spokesman added: “Our approach remains the same: we continue offering a range of prices and plans to meet a variety of needs, and as we deliver more value to our members, we reinvest in quality entertainment and improve their experience by updating our prices.”

Netflix, which has more than an estimated 18 million subscribers in the UK, previously raised its prices in February last year. The changes apply to new and existing customers.

The price rises are the latest of several borne by subscribers to streaming services.

Research by Ampere Analysis in August showed that Western Europe experienced the biggest average monthly increases across all streaming services in the past three years, at $1.86 (£1.38) or 16pc.

This was more than the $1.70 increase that subscribers faced in the US, the world’s biggest streaming market.

Amazon Prime Video, Disney+ and Paramount+ have all increased their prices in recent years, with the latter increasing the monthly cost of its ad-free premium plan last year to £14.99.

At the same time, many of the streaming giants are expanding their cheaper, ad-supported packages as they seek to keep revenues growing.

This week’s increases also underscore Netflix’s pricing power even as competition in the streaming market intensifies.

Netflix is planning to diversify into new forms of media such as podcasts, gaming and short-form videos to stay ahead of its competitors. It is also exploring live sports and ad breaks, the staples of traditional broadcast television.

Britain’s traditional broadcasters in turn face growing pressure from Netflix and other streaming services for viewers and advertising revenue. In August, it emerged that Netflix’s UK sales eclipsed those of ITV for the first time.

The streaming giant’s revenue topped £2bn last year, while ITV’s broadcast and streaming division made £1.9bn.

The company reported global revenues of $12.6bn in the second quarter of this year and quarterly net income of $3.4bn.

data.title: Boots in £7.5bn sale talks with billionaire family behind Primark
data.description:
Boots is in talks to sell itself for £7.5bn to the family behind Primark and an Australian pharmacy chain.

The billionaire Weston family, which owns Primark, is weighing up a bid that would see the chemist scrap plans for a London listing, according to the Financial Times.

The retail giant is understood to be in talks alongside Sigma Healthcare, an Australian pharmacy group, about a possible takeover of the 177-year-old chemist from Sycamore Partners, its private equity owner.

A takeover of Boots would derail plans for a stock market listing. The recent appointment of Alex Baldock – the former Currys boss credited with turning around the electronics retailer – as chief executive had fuelled speculation that Boots was being prepared to join the London Stock Market. 

Insiders had previously suggested that a flotation valuing the chain at up to £7bn was “always the plan”.

News of the talks came as Boots revealed that profits jumped by a quarter to £337m last year, as demand for weight-loss jabs, vaccinations and beauty products helped drive sales growth.

The Westons are one of the world’s richest retail families. Through their sprawling business empire they already control Primark-owner Associated British Foods (ABF), as well as Fortnum & Mason and major supermarket and pharmacy chains in Canada.

A deal would also deepen the family’s ties to British retail just months after it unveiled plans to split Primark from ABF, ending a six-decade partnership between the fashion chain and the conglomerate’s food operations.

Sigma, meanwhile, is a fast-growing Australian healthcare group best known for its links to Chemist Warehouse, Australia’s largest pharmacy retailer.

It has recently signalled ambitions to expand internationally and only last month entered the UK market through a pharmacy joint venture in and around London.

Hundreds of stores closed

A sale of Boots has been talked about for years. Walgreens first tried to offload it in 2022, before abandoning the effort when bids failed to meet expectations.

Sycamore Partners revived expectations of a breakup when it bought Walgreens Boots Alliance last year and carved out Boots as a standalone unit.

Boots has spent the past two years trying to improve its attractiveness to potential bidders. 

It has closed hundreds of under-performing UK stores as part of a broader cost-cutting drive, including a programme to shut branches, trimming its footprint from about 2,200 stores to roughly 1,900 in 2024.

At the same time, the chain has benefited from a boom in private healthcare services and a push into premium beauty brands, with online sales also rising sharply as more shoppers turned to its app and delivery partnerships.

The Weston family already has a presence in the pharmacy sector through Shoppers Drug Mart, a Canadian chain with more than 1,300 locations that it acquired in a multibillion-pound deal more than a decade ago.

Boots declined to comment.

data.title: One in eight Britons to take weight loss drugs by 2027
data.description:
One in eight Britons will be taking weight loss drugs by 2027, a new report has predicted.

The number of UK adults taking glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) weight loss medication will more than double from three million to seven million by next year, according to analysis by consulting firm PwC Strategy&, accounting for 13pc of the population.

This uptick will be fuelled by the approval of a new Wegovy pill, which will make weight loss treatment easier and more accessible.

This is expected to trigger a sharp drop in the sale of sweets and crisps, according to PwC, as the rollout dramatically changes consumer spending patterns.

Those already taking the medication cut their spending on snacks and sweet treats by 70pc and spent 60pc less on sugary drinks, PwC Strategy& found in a survey of more than 2,300 adults.

The latest findings have been released just weeks after the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) approved a tablet version of the blockbuster weight loss drug Wegovy.

This is the UK’s first GLP-1 pill for weight loss and can now be prescribed to adults with obesity.

It means that millions of Britons can access GLP-1 drugs, which mimic gut hormones to regulate people’s appetites, without needing to administer them by a weekly injection.

The pills will soon be rolled out across major retailers including Boots, Morrisons and Superdrug.

However, they are not yet available on the NHS. Before this can happen, the pill will need to be evaluated by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

While businesses selling confectionery or fast food will suffer from a drop-off in spending on unhealthy foods, those selling healthy products are likely to see a surge in sales.

GLP-1 users spent 60pc more on fresh food, 54pc more on high-protein options and 40pc more on vitamins and supplements, PwC Strategy& found.

They also spent 30pc more on fitness and an additional 40pc on clothing.

These spending patterns are likely to continue even after they have lost weight and stopped taking the drugs.

More than 80pc of those who had stopped treatment said they maintained at least some of the dietary changes they had made while taking the GLP-1s.

Jacqueline Windsor, head of retail at PwC UK, said: “GLP-1 is the most consumerised medication today. Who your GLP-1 customers are, and how your category changes, will dictate how brands and retailers compete.

“We’ll see consumer businesses reshape their portfolios to manage near-term risk.”

More than a quarter (28pc) of GLP-1 users said they would maintain their current levels of spending on the drugs even if the cost of living rose.

The drugs, which are only prescribed on the NHS for those with severe obesity, have predominantly been purchased by wealthier households, but are becoming increasingly mainstream.

Of current users, 6pc came from lower-income households, compared to 20pc for wealthier households.

Adoption of weight loss drugs has so far been highest among women, who account for 60pc of current users.

data.title: Reform promises tax-free buy-to-let homes
data.description:
Reform has promised to deliver tax-free new homes in an effort to revive the buy-to-let market and boost housebuilding.

The party will launch a consultation on making homes built on so-called brownfield sites free of stamp duty, capital gains tax and tax on rental income for a decade, Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, will announce at Reform’s party conference on Thursday.

Mr Tice told The Telegraph he wanted the measures to spur a new wave of buy-to-let investment and said the policies could unlock an additional 20,000 new homes per year on former industrial and commercial sites.

This would be a boost of about 10pc on current national building rates.

Mr Tice said: “It would be very tax-attractive. It would be the property equivalent of an Isa. We think that will stimulate a whole load of people to say, ‘I can build up a bit of a rental portfolio.’”

Reform also plans to scrap affordable housing requirements for developments on brownfield sites, or previously developed land, outside London, Birmingham, Manchester and Leeds.

This would mean getting rid of the so-called Section 106 contributions, which developers have to make as part of their planning applications and fund more than half of all affordable housing delivered in England.

Reform estimated that the exemptions would cost just over £1bn in lost tax receipts.

‘Business day’ at conference

Mr Tice made the announcement on “business day” at the Reform UK conference, as the party seeks to win over bosses by presenting a credible economic plan for Britain.

Reform is targeting housebuilding as Labour struggles to deliver on Sir Keir Starmer’s election campaign promise to construct 1.5 million new homes by 2029.

Although Labour moved quickly on planning reform in 2024, its measures have been nowhere near enough to counteract the toll of soaring building costs and plunging buyer demand.

Speaking at Reform’s party conference, Mr Tice said: “Planning, it takes too long. It’s too expensive, and the risk is too high too early in the process. And that’s led to what we’re seeing today, which is a collapse in the number of housing completions all over the country. We’ve got a planning crisis.”

Planning consents for new homes slumped to a two-decade low of 180,000 last year, and have fallen by a quarter since Labour came to power. The Government is on track to miss its target by more than half.

Mr Tice said: “Town centres are in a state of national crisis, and there’s too much greenfield development. There’s not enough brownfield development. We want to make brownfield sites much more attractive to developers.

“Money is so tight, the Government can’t give any grants or subsidies. What it can do is give tax incentives.

“If someone builds a new residential unit on a brownfield site, then there would be no stamp duty, no capital gains tax and no rental income tax, whether it is held personally or corporately, for a decade.”

Targeting brownfield sites for development was a key focus for the Tories, particularly under Boris Johnson, but the idea has been repeatedly criticised because the land is often the most complicated and expensive to develop.

Reform would also water down restrictions on listed buildings, making it easier to refurbish or change the internals of Grade II listed buildings.

Mr Tice said: “We have the courage to say that certain things ... are well intentioned but have been used by clever lawyers for the detriment of progress and in particular detrimental to building affordable housing in areas that need help.

“We have the courage to say, we love our listed buildings, but actually they do need to be used. What’s the point of having a huge, grade II listed building near my constituency that’s say there for 20 years, when it could accommodate hundreds, but because of restrictions it is too difficult?”

Support for the high street

As part of the consultation paper, Reform will also examine introducing a tax on online deliveries to encourage shoppers to go to their local high street instead.

Mr Tice said: “We’re looking at the concept of a modest delivery tax of 1pc to 2pc, for example, which would be on any online delivery, whether it is a kebab or buying a pair of jeans.

“If I order a pair of jeans online, I would pay a delivery tax of 1pc to 2pc, or I could go to the town centre and not pay that, try it on, and have the joy of nipping out for a coffee at the same time.”

Reform also plans to lift the threshold for business rates in town centres, a move that would reduce bills for physical shops.

Mr Tice added: “Some of the big out-of-town warehouses, they’re getting away too lightly on the amount of rates that they pay. So we’re going to do some rebalancing. Town centres have been hollowed out and there has to be an adjustment for that.”

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Volkswagen to slash up to 50,000 jobs
data.description:
Volkswagen’s shares have surged after the German giant confirmed plans to cut 50,000 jobs as it battles competition from China.

The carmaker’s Frankfurt-listed shares jumped by more than 8pc on Friday after it unveiled the sweeping job cuts, which are the biggest in Volkswagen’s 89-year history.

Volkswagen said on Thursday it would cut tens of thousands more roles as it faces fierce competition from Chinese rivals that are flooding into Europe.

The German carmaker said that the restructuring would be in addition to 50,000 reductions that it has already made since 2024 and could lead to plant closures.

It is racing to cut costs as it grapples with fierce competition from Chinese rivals such as BYD and slowing demand in Europe. It has also struggled under US tariffs and Volkswagen vehicle sales fell by 8.4pc in the first half of the year, while its operating profit dropped by 11.6pc.

News of the restructuring plans emerged earlier this year, but had yet to be approved by Volkswagen’s supervisory board, which represents the labour force and shareholders.

The carmaker said its European capacity “currently exceeds demand by more than 500,000 units”. The new plan will pave the way for Volkswagen to slim its vehicle line-up by as much as 50pc by 2035.

“Given intensifying global competition, shifting demand and technological change in the automotive industry, a consistent alignment of workforce capacity with economic reality is essential,” the company said in a statement.

Last September, Porsche, which is owned by Volkswagen, blamed a decision to delay the launch of its new electric SUV in September on weak demand for electric cars as it warned of a €5.1bn (£4.4bn) hit to profits.

Volkswagen added that it could not guarantee that a number of its plants would be used from 2030 onwards. It said it was considering alternative uses for the four affected factories. Some could potentially be converted into use by Germany’s defence industry.

Oliver Blume, the Volkswagen chief executive, said last month that the company was in talks with defence companies to use its site in Osnabrück.

The new cuts represent about 8pc of the company’s global workforce of roughly 650,000 across brands such as Škoda, Seat, Porsche and Lamborghini.

It comes after lengthy talks between the company, its unions and Lower Saxony, the German state where the company is headquartered. The state is also a large minority shareholder in Volkswagen.

Mr Blume has previously said that Volkswagen needed to rein in costs, which were roughly 30pc higher than its competitors. The company said it was seeking to lift its margin to 9pc by 2030, up from just 3.8pc in the first half of this year.

In a statement, he said that the new cost-cutting plans were “a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group”.

“We are taking responsibility for our entire workforce, for our partners and for industrial jobs worldwide,” he added.

data.title: Shein shares plunge on stock market debut
data.description:
Shares in Shein have plunged on their first day of trading on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

The fast-fashion giant’s stock price fell by as much as 10pc on Tuesday as it made a long-awaited stock-market debut.

The online retailer was once estimated to be worth almost $100bn (£74bn). However, the slump saw Shein valued at just $24bn by the end of Tuesday’s trading session in Asia.

The underwhelming launch suggests that the London Stock Exchange may have dodged a bullet. Shein had considered listing in the UK. Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, lobbied Shein to join hoping that its listing could help revive the moribund market.

However, the company’s plans to float in both New York and London were derailed by a backlash from politicians and human rights groups over its alleged use of forced labour in China. Shein has previously said it “strictly prohibits forced labour” in its supply chain.

While Shein’s shares plunged by as much as 10pc in Hong Kong, the stock recovered some ground to end the session down 4pc.

The fall comes as Shein’s business model comes under pressure from regulatory changes around the world.

New fees on the import of small packages into the US have hit Shein’s sales after Donald Trump removed the “de minimis exemptions” on imports worth less than $800, which meant they were exempt from tax.

Shein reported a $99m loss in the first three months of this year, blaming a hit to its American sales.

The EU introduced similar changes in July, by placing a €3 (£2.50) tax on deliveries worth less than €150, which were previously exempt from import levies. The UK is planning to make similar changes by March 2029.

Human rights concerns

At the same time, Shein has faced new competition from companies such as Temu.

Shein was started in Nanjing in 2008 and became popular for selling cheap clothes shipped from its network of factories in China. It grew rapidly to become one of the world’s biggest clothes sellers, on par with European giants Zara and H&M.

Shein, which shifted its headquarters to Singapore in 2022, filed for an initial public offering on the London stock market in 2024. However, it was derailed by scrutiny from MPs and amid pressure from the US over the company’s alleged links to forced labour.

The company similarly abandoned plans to float in New York after experiencing intense backlash, including over its alleged use of cotton from the Xinjiang region where the Muslim Uyghur population has been forced into manual labour.

Shein was started by Chris Xu, a Chinese entrepreneur, who is now one of the richest people in China with a net worth of $11bn, according to Bloomberg.
