data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Sports Direct in row with advertising watchdog over ‘false’ discounts
data.description:
Mike Ashley’s Sports Direct has accused the advertising watchdog of being “out of touch” in a deepening row over discounting at the cut-price retailer.

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) banned an advert displayed on the sports chain’s website, ruling that its use of recommended retail prices (RRP) was misleading.

The ad promoted a £17 Puma baselayer top that was advertised as reduced from a £45 RRP, with Sports Direct claiming shoppers could get “up to 50pc off”.

Sports Direct said Puma had confirmed the £45 RRP had been in place since at least 2023 and that the top had previously been sold by the manufacturer at that price.

But the regulator said this did not prove that £45 was the price at which the product was generally sold across the market.

It noted that the same top was available for £17 from another Frasers Group retailer and for £23 from another sports retailer. It concluded that the evidence did not support the claim that £45 was a genuine market price against which shoppers could judge their savings.

The watchdog told Sports Direct to withdraw the advert and warned that future savings claims must be based on genuine market prices.

Sports Direct criticised the ruling and vowed to “contest it fully”.

The company said: “The ASA’s ‘out of touch’ approach to the use of RRPs is fundamentally flawed. We do not accept that it is the valid legal test for whether an RRP is misleading or not, or that it reflects consumers’ understanding of RRPs, which have been around for many decades.”

It argued that the watchdog’s approach was unworkable for retailers, who would have to gather pricing data from across the market to justify every RRP they used.

‘Yet more regulation’

The spat came days after Mr Ashley, the owner of Sports Direct’s parent company Frasers Group, attacked Andy Burnham’s plans to crack down on “rip-off” discounts.

The Prime Minister has pledged to review the use of misleading RRPs as part of efforts to tackle unfair practices on the high street.

Writing to Mr Burnham last week, Mr Ashley said RRPs were a well-established basis for pricing and that driving down prices through discounting helped consumers get better value.

He accused Mr Burnham of relying on the “old salve of yet more regulation”, arguing that the focus should instead be on rising business costs.

The ASA published updated guidance on RRPs last month, warning retailers not to rely solely on a manufacturer’s recommended price when making savings claims.

It is not the first time the advertising watchdog has intervened in discounting claims made by retailers.

In a 2022 ruling against Lidl, it accepted an RRP for a vacuum cleaner where three other retailers were selling it at that price, but rejected RRPs for other products where Lidl could point only to the manufacturer and one retailer.

Sports Direct said its approach was designed to give customers the lowest possible prices and insisted it was acting in their interests during the cost of living crisis.

data.title: Vodafone has a solution to Britain’s woeful mobile internet – but it’ll cost you
data.description:
Vodafone and Three have unveiled a 5G service to counteract Britain’s sluggish mobile coverage, but customers must pay a premium to use it.

VodafoneThree – formed following a £15bn merger between the networks last year – is launching a new service offering speeds up to four times faster than its standard network.

It will also offer minimum speeds of 15 megabits per second – fast enough to stream high-definition video – in a first for the industry.

The move is aimed at tackling lacklustre mobile internet service across the UK, which ranks bottom among G7 nations for both speed and coverage. Andrea Dona, Vodafone’s chief network officer, described Britain’s performance as “embarrassing”.

Vodafone contract customers will have to pay an extra £3 per month to access the improved service, while those on SIM-only and handset plans will have to pay up to £12 more a month.

Max Taylor, the chief executive of VodafoneThree, said: “We think that’s great value for money to get the benefits of enhanced speed, greater reliability and security bundled in.”

UK mobile network operators have been under growing pressure from politicians and customers to stamp out sluggish connections and so-called signal “not spots”.

Research by mobile data firm Streetwave earlier this year found that almost half the country struggled to browse the internet, though mobile companies have disputed the findings.

VodafoneThree’s improved mobile offering, called SuperMobile, will be provided through technology known as “slicing”, which allows different parts of a mobile network to be used for different purposes.

Users who pay extra will also be prioritised, meaning they are more likely to have signal in busy areas such as city centres and at events such as concerts and sports fixtures.

Bosses insisted that non-priority customers would continue to access the network as normal and would not be deprioritised as a result of the new offering.

VodafoneThree said the move was possible thanks to its expanded holdings of mobile spectrum following last year’s merger.

At the time of the merger, Vodafone said its 5G upgrades would come at no extra cost, while the company made a number of commitments over tariffs to assuage the regulator’s concerns about higher prices.

Bosses insisted that all customers would benefit from improved quality as the company invests £11bn in its combined network, adding that the new 5G service was an optional extra for those willing to pay a premium.

TV challenger

VodafoneThree also announced plans for a new TV service on Thursday, to lure more customers to its broadband service.

Vodafone TV, which launches next month, will offer access to HBO Max and Netflix, as well as the streaming platforms of British broadcasters such as the BBC, ITV and Channel 4. Additional streaming services can be accessed at an extra cost.

Mr Taylor added: “Vodafone SuperMobile is tangible evidence of what the Vodafone and Three merger makes possible: better connectivity and real choice for customers.

“The UK needs to go faster and with the country’s largest, best spectrum holding and our £11bn investment, we will build a faster, higher-quality network than anyone else.”

data.title: Britain to build turbines for Rolls-Royce mini-nuclear reactors
data.description:
British workers will build steam turbines for Rolls-Royce’s fleet of mini-nuclear reactors in a boost to domestic manufacturing.

Siemens Energy will produce the huge machines for a new generation of small modular reactors (SMRs) at its factory in Newcastle.

They will be used in the three Rolls-designed SMRs that are being built in Anglesey, as well as further reactors set to be built in the Czech Republic and Sweden.

It will be the first time large steam turbines have been made domestically in more than 20 years.

The expansion will follow an investment in the Newcastle factory understood to be worth tens of millions of pounds. It is expected to create 550 jobs.

It follows concerns raised by MPs that SMR components were set to be built abroad.

Rolls-Royce SMR said the decision by German engineering giant Siemens demonstrated how the company was “delivering its commitment to localisation, driving investment and re-shoring work that would have taken place overseas”.

Rolls-Royce SMR is an independent company, majority owned by Rolls-Royce but with investors including Qatar and France’s Perrodo family.

Chris Cholerton, the company’s chief executive, said: “We are building on a remarkable industrial legacy while creating and sustaining the skills and supply chain needed to deliver clean, secure and affordable energy for decades to come.”

Darren Davidson, of Siemens Energy, added: “We’re preparing to manufacture the next generation of steam turbines for small modular reactors, supporting energy security, creating skilled jobs and helping power the UK’s future energy mix.”

The Government awarded Rolls a contract to design and develop Britain’s first three SMRs last year.

They will be built in Anglesey, North Wales, in a project aimed at proving the commercial viability of the still-nascent technology by the mid-2030s. Each one will generate 470 megawatts of power.

Rolls selected Siemens Energy as its supplier of steam turbines last year, but there had been uncertainty about where the key components would be manufactured until now.

The British company faced a backlash earlier this year after it emerged that some other parts would be made overseas, including reactor pressure vessels that will be imported from either South Korea or the Czech Republic.

Labour ministers have set a target for 70pc of components to be made in Britain, and on Thursday they hailed the announcement by Siemens as proof their plan to “reindustrialise Britain” was working.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, said: “Producing these components here in the UK will help strengthen our energy security, reduce our exposure to volatile international gas markets, create new export opportunities for British industry, and reindustrialise the UK.”

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, added: “Building small modular reactors here in the UK presents huge benefits for us, from more export opportunities to more jobs on the ground at home.”

The Newcastle factory is expected to make both high-pressure turbines and valve casings.

It will also become the service hub for the turbines in the Rolls SMR fleet, ensuring a pipeline of work for the site that is expected to last decades.

The historic Parsons Works is the site once run by Sir Charles Parsons, the revered British engineer who helped to revolutionise marine propulsion with his invention of the multi-stage steam turbine.

It was established in 1889 and was where the steam turbine for Calder Hall – the world’s first commercial nuclear power station, in Cumbria – was built.

Grid-scale steam turbines have not been manufactured in the UK since the early 2000s, when Siemens scaled back its operations in Newcastle.

A steam turbine for a nuclear power plant has not been built in Britain since the early 1990s when one was supplied for the Sizewell B plant in Suffolk.

Tom Greatrex, of the Nuclear Industry Association, said: “This is what reindustrialisation looks like: a vital clean energy project reviving our old manufacturing capabilities to provide good, skilled jobs where we need them.

“The announcement is a real vote of confidence in industrial Britain and shows what SMRs and nuclear projects can deliver for this country.”

data.title: Trump backs OpenAI in copyright battle with New York Times
data.description:
The Trump administration has thrown its weight behind OpenAI in the ChatGPT maker’s copyright battle with The New York Times (NYT).

Lawyers for the US government have submitted a “statement of interest” intervening in the newspaper’s lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft.

NYT claims OpenAI and Microsoft used its articles to train AI bots without permission, claiming the tech companies were seeking to “free ride” on its journalism.

In a 20-page statement submitted to the court, US lawyers said that it was “critical for the United States to retain global leadership in artificial intelligence”. They warned that blocking tech companies from using copyrighted work would threaten national security.

“Rules of law that make it significantly more difficult to develop a robust AI industry in the United States ... threaten national security and give a competitive advantage to foreign adversaries who are not so encumbered,” they wrote.

Publishers, musicians and artists have claimed that AI companies are breaking copyright laws by ingesting large amounts of text, music and video to train their systems.

The companies say that under US law, they are protected by “fair use” rules.

The Trump administration said that requiring AI companies to seek permission for all content used in training would harm the economy.

“Constraining LLM development under a misunderstanding of fair use doctrine would thwart such creative and scientific progress, while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility,” its lawyers wrote.

The NYT sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, a year after the release of ChatGPT. This summer, it said Microsoft had encouraged OpenAI to steal its content. The newspaper claims that the infringements have allowed ChatGPT to compete as a source of information.

The tech companies deny wrongdoing.

OpenAI rival Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5bn (£1.11bn) last year to book publishers after a judge found it had illegally downloaded and saved millions of books.

A flurry of other lawsuits from music labels and publishers have been filed since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

The companies are to submit arguments to the judge before potential rulings in the coming months. The lawsuit could lead to a trial next year.

Donald Trump has consistently backed AI companies in the copyright clash.

“You can’t be expected to have a successful AI program when every single article, book, or anything else that you’ve read or studied, you’re supposed to pay for. ‘Gee, I read a book. I’m supposed to pay somebody,’” he said in a speech last year.

“When a person reads a book or an article, you’ve gained great knowledge. That does not mean that you’re violating copyright laws or have to make deals with every content provider.”

data.title: Volkswagen’s troubles are far from over
data.description:
It is the “fundamental breakthrough” the company needs, according to Deutsche Bank. It is a “brave and realistic” plan, according to Citibank.

Analysts and investors were quick to back Volkswagen after it announced 100,000 jobs would be cut in a radical restructuring plan agreed by the board on Friday.

The carmaker is completely right to finally start tackling the crisis that has engulfed it. Yet it will have to go a lot further to turn the business around – and it is certainly far too early for shareholders to bet on a decisive recovery.

Five years ago, even the suggestion of any redundancies at all at Volkswagen would have been unimaginable. Now they are happening on a vast scale. The company announced on Friday that another 50,000 people would go, taking the total to 100,000 by the end of this decade, out of around 600,000 employees.

The number of models across the group – which includes Škoda, Audi and Porsche as well as the main Volkswagen brand – will be halved and up to four factories may be closed.

“This is a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen group,” said Oliver Blume, Volkswagen’s chief executive, announcing that the board had agreed to the plan. “Over the coming years, we will invest a three-figure billion sum to make our iconic brands even more attractive, stronger and more competitive.”

No one can criticise Blume for putting the most optimistic spin he can on his turnaround strategy. He is just doing his job.

For the moment, the stock market appears willing to buy into his optimistic forecasts. On Friday morning, Volkswagen’s shares were up by 7pc, although they are still down by 60pc in the last five years.

“It is a much-better-than-feared outcome,” said Deutsche Bank in a note. “We expect the market to react positively.”

Well, perhaps. The trouble is, while the plan is certainly bold, there is a lot of hard work still to be done if Volkswagen is to be saved in anything like its present shape.

Sure, it is a solution of sorts. By shifting investment to the premium models such as Audi and Porsche, by reducing its sprawling complexity – it is hard to believe anyone ever thought it was a good idea to have 130 models within a single company in the first place – and by cutting its least efficient factories, Volkswagen may well be able to stabilise its finances and stop the relentless decline in its overall sales. But it does not address the heart of the problem.

In reality, what used to be Europe’s largest manufacturing business – at least as measured by sales – faces three huge challenges.

To start with, Germany’s energy and labour costs remain far too high for a company of this size to stay competitive. Industrial energy in Germany now costs 50pc more than in France and three times what it costs in the US or China.

It is only in comparison with Britain that it looks competitive – but of course, we hardly make any cars any more, or indeed much else, come to think of it. Compared with any other country, the energy costs are crippling.

Labour costs are almost as bad. Only last month, the German Economic Institute reported that unit labour costs in Germany were 22pc higher than an average of 27 industrialised countries. You can install all the robots on the shop floor you want but it is hard to overcome that kind of difference, especially when you are employing more than half a million people.

Let’s keep in mind that Volkswagen is the world’s third-largest manufacturing employer. The two above it are in China (BYD) and Taiwan (Foxconn), where labour costs a lot less. It is hard to see that the conglomerate will be much more viable with 500,000 people earning a lot more than the global average than it was with 600,000.

Next, it has fallen hopelessly behind in electric vehicles (EVs). We can all debate about how quickly the market will switch to battery-powered cars or whether they are the right technology to deal with climate change. But there is little question that they will account for a huge chunk of the market.

In July this year, EVs took a quarter of the European market for new vehicles. And yet for all the millions spent on research, the EV market basically belongs to Tesla and to the new Chinese manufacturers, led by BYD, Chery and SAIC. It is going to take a lot more work and a lot of investment to remain competitive in that sector.

Finally, it is going to struggle in the global market. Donald Trump is determined to use tariffs to lock up the American market for domestically manufactured cars, while China is intent on building up its own emerging giants. That is starting to hurt. In the second quarter of this year, Volkswagen’s sales in China were down by 37pc, dragging down the whole group.

With the world’s biggest and second-biggest economies both increasingly closed for foreign auto manufacturers and with China’s super-cheap cars dominating the developing markets, Volkswagen is going to have to mainly rely on Europe. But with an ageing population and low growth, that is going to be a very tough slog.

The stock market is acting as if cutting 100,000 jobs has fixed all of Volkswagen’s problems. With fewer people and greater efficiency, it can get back to where it was 10 years ago, slugging it out with Toyota to dominate the global industry. It is a reassuring story.

The trouble is, it is not really true. The brutal truth is that those days are long gone. Volkswagen has finally made a start on fixing its crisis but it will have to go a lot further if there is to be any kind of meaningful recovery.

data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: Flooding to cause rail chaos
data.description:
Flash flooding is expected to cause rail chaos after weeks of drought, train bosses have warned.

Network Rail said it expected delays and cancellations because rail tracks are susceptible to being flooded when rainfall runs off dry, hard ground.

It comes after the Met Office issued thunderstorm warnings for parts of Britain on Wednesday and Thursday, warning of flash-flooding risks.

Craig Snell, a senior Met Office meteorologist, said the wetter conditions created a risk of flooding as heavy showers fell on baked, dry ground.

He said: “Parts of the North West have seen some localised flooding, and also parts of the south coast of England over the last 24 hours or so. Part of that is down to the fact that the rain is falling on quite baked ground, so the water is not sinking in like it would usually do.”

Network Rail is preparing for disruption, it is understood. Speed restrictions or suspensions are imposed on train services when flood water rises above rails, meaning storms could lead to delays and cancellations.

The Met Office said showers were expected to continue near the coast on Thursday evening, but would probably fade across inland areas overnight, with clear spells developing elsewhere.

Further showers were forecast in most parts of the UK for Friday, but were not expected to be as widespread or heavy as they were on Thursday in many areas. Some thunderstorms were also expected overnight across parts of Wales and western England.

A Network Rail spokesman said: “We are not predicting major disruption from flooding in the short or longer term this year. However, we are not complacent. 

“Our long-range forecast suggests it will be a warm, wet winter – in line with climate change predictions for Britain – and we are doing all we can to be ready for that. A programme of improving the railway’s resilience is ongoing.”

Meanwhile, a railway line on which a train derailed last week is set to remain closed until September.  A London Victoria to Eastbourne service derailed near Lewes station on Aug 13, trapping passengers in carriages. Thirty were injured, with 20 requiring hospital treatment.

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) said investigators would explore whether the record-breaking spell of high temperatures and dry weather “in the weeks and months” leading to the accident had contributed to it.

On Aug 13, temperatures reached 38.1C in west London. The RAIB noted that there had been “a sustained period of hot and dry weather” before the accident. Experts said the rails at the site of the derailment had been known to be misaligned beforehand.

Network Rail and Southern Rail said the line between Lewes and Haywards Heath would remain closed until Sept 1 while the train was recovered and the track was repaired.

data.title: Reform drums up business support at conference
data.description:
Large firms are flocking to Reform UK’s national conference as the party prepares to host its inaugural business day.

First Bus, BT, Vodafone, Google, Heathrow, JCB, Dubai Ports and TikTok are among the businesses sponsoring or running events at the three-day summit which starts on Thursday in Birmingham.

The party’s decision to host a business day forms part of a wider Reform UK strategy to replace the Conservatives as the main opposition party to Andy Burnham’s government by fighting Labour on economic grounds.

In recent weeks, the party has unveiled plans for the biggest welfare shake-up “in a generation” by scrapping key benefits to save £50bn a year, more than double what the Tories plan to save, as well as pledging a £30 rebate for taxpayers stuck on hold to His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs (HMRC).

To appeal to wealthy backers, they are also offering conference packages worth up to £3,000, which include a champagne breakfast with Nigel Farage, an opportunity to meet and network with senior Reform leaders and a three-course meal in the Platinum hospitality area.

‘Increased engagement’

The party has toned down its offerings from last year in an attempt to professionalise, scrapping offers of custom cocktail naming rights and the delivery of bottles of sparkling wine to business stands.

A Reform UK spokesman told The Telegraph: “Engagement from British business has increased significantly. Companies across the country recognise they need to understand Reform and what a future Reform government could mean for them.

“Businesses now realise that the possibility of a Reform government is very real and are acting accordingly.”

Until 2025, Reform had a relatively low attendance from big business compared with similar events organised by Labour and the Tories.

But the influx of big business to this year’s annual event signals that the corporate world is taking the possibility of a Reform government seriously, as the party continues to outperform rivals in voter intention polling.

Crypto sidelined

Reform, which topped polls for almost 16 consecutive months between March 2025 and July 2026 and won hundreds of councillors in May, is now in second place trailing the Labour Party following a so-called Burnham bounce.

Meanwhile, Mr Farage is also believed to be sidelining crypto companies in favour of mainstream corporates following a backlash over the Reform leader’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, the Bitcoin billionaire.

Crypto companies are not among the businesses sponsoring the 2026 conference, which last year included donations from crypto payments firm Zebec.

The party has also scrapped perks it had previously offered to crypto industry leaders, including free tickets and access to senior figures, according to City AM, in a notable departure from previous years.

Conferences and the sponsorship fees that come in from big businesses are one of the ways that political parties raise revenue for their campaigning efforts.

A Heathrow spokesman said the airport had “a long history of constructive engagement across the political spectrum”.

He said: “Like many businesses – from airlines to pubs and banks to supermarkets – it is common practice to sponsor events at party conferences to engage policymakers and ensure they better understand the needs of consumers and the economy.”

data.title: M&S and Tesco warn Burnham against high street tax raid
data.description:
Retail giants, including Marks & Spencer and Tesco, have warned Andy Burnham that further tax rises would damage his plans to revive Britain’s high streets.

The Retail Jobs Alliance, which also counts Asda, Morrisons, Primark and Sainsbury’s among its members, said any move to increase taxes on large shops would put retailers under further pressure at a time of rising costs and could lead to higher prices for customers.

In a letter to the Prime Minister, the group said: “Retail stores are integral to high street renaissance, but they cannot continue investing in communities if they face an ever-increasing tax burden.”

Retailers fear that ministers could increase the business rates paid by shops whose rateable value – a measure used to determine how much property tax they pay – is above £500,000.

About 4,000 stores fall into this category, employing one in three retail workers.

It is thought the tax increase would be used to fund Mr Burnham’s plans to cut business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues as part of his drive to revive high streets.

In his first speech in the Commons since becoming Prime Minister, Mr Burnham said on Tuesday: “For 40 years, too many places have been drifting.

“Too many British high streets tell the story of this decline. People yearn to see them restored to what they once were.”

But the retail consortium urged the Government to exempt bricks-and-mortar stores from a higher business rates charge.

Bosses warned that further tax increases would hit investment, jobs and the viability of the large stores, which act as anchors for town centres.

They added that higher taxes would make it harder for retailers to keep prices low, potentially undermining Labour’s efforts to ease the cost of living.

The retailers said the high street was a “single ecosystem”, with shops, pubs, restaurants and other businesses all relying on footfall and consumer spending.

They warned that cutting the rates burden for hospitality while increasing it for retailers risked undermining the very town-centre investment the Government was trying to encourage.

‘Most important pathways’

The letter was also signed by Usdaw, the retail union with around 370,000 members and one of Labour’s biggest financial backers.

The warning comes as John Healey, the Chancellor, seeks ideas from businesses, economists and other organisations on how to boost economic growth as he prepares his first Budget in October.

The alliance said the retail sector already pays 21pc of all business rates despite accounting for only 5pc of GDP.

It added that last year’s autumn Budget had imposed £7bn in new costs and taxes on the sector, with further increases likely to feed through into prices and put pressure on employment and investment.

The retailers also pointed to the role they play in giving young people work opportunities as the Government examined how to tackle rising youth unemployment.

The alliance said: “Retail remains one of the country’s most important pathways into work for young people.

“As the Milburn review examines rising youth unemployment and Neets [young people not in employment, education or training], it is vital to protect these routes into employment.”

It came as Sir Sadiq Khan separately backed calls for the Government to restore tax-free shopping for overseas visitors.

The Mayor of London said the abolition of tax-free shopping had left Britain lagging behind rival European cities on visitor spending.

He said: “London is a globally renowned tourist destination, but the decision to remove tax-free shopping by the previous Government was a huge mistake, which has led to us trailing behind other European cities on visitor spending for too long.

“With growth at the top of this Government’s agenda, and the evidence showing that the benefits would extend beyond retail to every part of the economy, the Government should consider using the autumn Budget to reinstate tax-free shopping and make it clear to the world that London and the UK is open for business.”

Research commissioned by the Heart of London Business Alliance found that bringing back VAT-free shopping could generate £11.5bn in economic output, support 153,000 jobs and deliver a £2.6bn net gain for the Treasury.

More than 500 business leaders have signed a letter calling for the policy to be reviewed in the Budget.

The Treasury was approached for comment.

data.title: Harvey Nichols’ former owner faces £100m loss from sale
data.description:
The billionaire former owner of Harvey Nichols was owed more than £100m when the luxury store group crashed into administration in August.

Sir Dickson Poon, a Hong Kong tycoon, is by far the biggest creditor to the upmarket fashion, cosmetics and food retailer through his company Broad Gain (UK), according to financial documents filed at Companies House on Thursday.

His company is owed £104.6m, and it is feared Sir Dickson is unlikely to recover much, if any, of the money he has poured into the retailer.

The UK operations of Harvey Nichols, best known for its “Harvey Nics” Knightsbridge flagship store, were acquired by Mike Ashley’s retail empire Frasers Group in a £43m pre-pack deal on Aug 13.

The sale also included five other stores in Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds, Edinburgh and Dublin, and all 993 employees were transferred with the change in ownership.

But the insolvency left hundreds of unsecured creditors, including many small suppliers, with unpaid bills totalling more than £240m.

The Notice of Administrator’s proposals, drawn up by insolvency specialists FTI Consulting (FTI), predict that unsecured creditors can only expect to recover between 0.01pc and 20pc of the amount they are out of pocket. The exact return will depend on which company within the Harvey Nichols group owes them the money.

The family of Sir Dickson, whose son Pearson Poon served as vice-chairman of Harvey Nichols, had ploughed substantial sums into the retail business he owned for 35 years in a doomed struggle to keep it afloat.

His latest support came in 2024 when the 70-year-old Hong Kong-based magnate lent the business another £32.5m.

Much of the funding was used to pay down bank debt, leaving the business dependent on its owner’s support.

But the 85-page report from Lindsay Hallam, Andrew Johnson and Matthew Callaghan, the joint administrators, laid bare how the retail landmark, made well known through its association with the 1990s sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, was facing a losing battle to stay afloat.

Management accounts for the most recent financial year show Harvey Nichols made a post-tax loss of £59m on sales of £173m, a margin of minus 35pc. Sales have slumped from £229m in 2024.

The report said trading had been hit by “a number of significant headwinds” over six years. These included the pandemic lockdowns, intense competition from online rivals, decreased high-street footfall and weak consumer demand.

This had been compounded by the removal of VAT-free shopping for foreigners – the so-called tourist tax – by Rishi Sunak, the former chancellor, from January 2021.

This resulted in “a marked reduction in visits from high net worth customers from across the Middle East and Asia”.

A new management team led by Julia Goddard, the chief executive, was installed in 2024, but it could not reverse the decline in trading. FTI was first appointed “to assess the liquidity position” in June.

Sir Dickson originally purchased Harvey Nichols from the Burton Group in 1991 for £53m. The company was floated on the stock exchange in 1996, but he took it private in 2002.

FTI and Harvey Nichols were approached for comment.

data.title: Sky accuses ex-Bake Off boss of double-counting costs in accounts row
data.description:
Sky has accused the TV producer behind The Great British Bake Off of double-counting costs in an escalating legal row about the hit show.

Letty Kavanagh, the former managing director of Love Productions, has launched a claim against Sky in the employment tribunal, alleging that the broadcaster drew up misleading financial accounts and then fired her when she blew the whistle.

She is also suing Sky in the High Court, alleging it owes her around £755,000 in severance payments.

But in its defence filed on Tuesday, Sky accused Ms Kavanagh of deliberately double-counting production costs in a way that artificially decreased profits at Love, which also makes The Piano and Benefits Street.

The pay-TV group said the former Love boss was “instrumental” in this double-counting, which is alleged to have occurred between June and September last year. It is alleged that she continued the practice even after her actions were questioned by finance executives at both Love and Sky.

Sky, which is owned by US cable giant Comcast, also alleges inappropriate use of a corporate credit card for personal expenses, including boat trips, taxi fares and international postal services.

A review conducted by Sky this year found that Ms Kavanagh’s actions amounted to gross misconduct and had therefore breached the conditions attached to the severance payment offer. As a result, the broadcaster argues that she is no longer entitled to the money.

A spokesman for Ms Kavanagh described the accusations as a “retrospective smear campaign”.

A source close to the TV producer denied allegations of double-counting, saying this was the result of “chaos” caused by accounting changes imposed by Sky.

They added that an assistant had accidentally used the wrong card to book a small boat for a holiday, but that Ms Kavanagh had offered to pay this back immediately.

The legal tussle underscores the parlous state of accounting at Love, which is now playing a crucial role in Sky’s £1.6bn takeover of ITV’s broadcasting arm. Dana Strong, Sky’s chief executive, is preparing to hand over the production company to ITV’s studios arm at a valuation of £200m.

Sky said the alleged false financial reporting was disclosed and corrected by Love’s finance team after Ms Kavanagh’s termination. It is understood that ITV is aware of the disputed accounting at the production company.

Ms Kavanagh was handed her notice and put on gardening leave in November 2025 after 18 years at Love.

She alleged that Sky imposed changes to the company’s accounts to create a more flattering financial picture and that she was dismissed after raising concerns. She claimed she was also ousted for blowing the whistle on Sky’s plan to poach Bake Off from Channel 4 and move the programme on to its own service.

The former executive has made a claim in the employment tribunal for unfair dismissal of a whistleblower and sex discrimination.

Her partner Kieran Smith, Love’s creative director, was also sacked shortly afterwards and has filed a parallel unfair dismissal claim.

Sky acknowledged that accounting changes were made, but maintained that these were legitimate and strongly rejected the allegations. The company said Ms Kavanagh’s claims about accounting were independently investigated after she was dismissed and not substantiated.

Sky’s filing also revealed that Ms Kavanagh received almost £6m in bonus payments between 2019 and 2024, including £2.5m in March 2020 linked to Sky’s acquisition of the remaining shares in Love.

A Sky spokesman said: “We wholly reject Ms Kavanagh’s claims and are confident in our position. We have taken the concerns she has raised seriously and sought throughout to deal with these matters fairly and appropriately.

“It is regrettable that this dispute has resulted in legal proceedings. Our defence sets out our position in full, and we will now respond to the claims through the legal process.”

A spokesman for Ms Kavanagh said: “This is a retrospective smear campaign designed to discredit a senior executive who spent over a year blowing the whistle on severe financial mismanagement, structural conflicts of interest and governance breaches by Sky.

“Letty looks forward to having the truth revealed in court – and shining a light on the ruthless corporate approach Sky/Comcast takes to its shows and the TV industry.”

data.title: Gas crisis threatens to blow up Germany’s fragile recovery
data.description:
Germany’s economy has shown surprising signs of strength lately. Consumer, investor and business confidence has rebounded, factories are taking more orders and growth is the fastest since 2022.

This wasn’t on most economists’ bingo cards for 2026. Beleaguered by high energy costs, cut-throat Chinese competition and swathes of red tape, Germany is perennially called “the sick man of Europe”.

But nobody is quite sure whether the patient is set to climb out of the sick bed. If you want to figure that out, you might be better off consulting a meteorologist rather than an economist.

Germany is standing on the precipice of a gas shortage that could drive up winter energy bills for already battered households and industry. That risks sending the barely reheated economy back into the deep freeze.

If there’s a mild winter, Germany might stumble through. But if the mercury plummets, then businesses and consumers could suffer a painful economic chill.

The reason why Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, will be anxiously watching his thermometer is that Germany has fallen behind in its annual summer race to fill the country’s gas storage tanks in time for winter.

The amount of gas in the storage facilities is the lowest for this time of year since records began in 2009.

“That storage gas is crucial to keeping lights on and people warm during the winter,” says Bill Farren-Price, of the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.

“You cannot simply import more liquefied natural gas at that point – the speed of delivery is not fast enough.”

The tanks are only 51pc full. By the start of November, the aim was to hit 70pc, but most forecasters reckon there’s now little chance of getting anywhere past 60pc by then.

“There is growing concern within the industry about potential supply shortages next winter,” warned Thilo Brodtmann, the head of the German industry body VDMA.

“A physical gas shortage or skyrocketing prices would pose a significant threat to industry.”

Shunning nuclear and coal, Germany relies heavily on gas and wind power. So if demand spikes in the cold weather and the wind isn’t turning the turbines, Germany will have to fill the resulting energy shortfall by buying gas on the spot market.

That could be painful. The European gas price, hit by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has surged to its highest level since the first winter of the Russia-Ukraine war.

In the winter months just before the Iran war started on Feb 28, the price was still between €30 (£26) and €40 per megawatt hour. But in the past month, the price has jumped close to 20pc, hitting almost €70.

Hamad Hussain, an analyst at Capital Economics, had been expecting the price to settle at €60 later this year. 

“But in the absence of a significant shift in the status quo, it is becoming more likely that prices could rise even further, perhaps towards €80 to €100,” he said in a note.

Buying gas at twice the price of last winter will send wholesale energy costs soaring.

“Companies would be hit first. And then it would be households, because they typically have multiple-year contracts that are normally adjusted or renewed at the start of the year,” says Carsten Brzeski, the global head of macro at Dutch bank ING.

German households already pay one third more for their electricity than the EU average and businesses pay one of the highest rates for energy on the Continent.

Both are struggling. German retail sales and industrial output have both shrunk over the past year and are among the weakest in the G7 economies.

With the economy growing just 0.3pc in the second quarter, Merz can ill afford to let energy costs climb any higher.

“As those costs do start to feed through, though, we wouldn’t be surprised to see activity slow in energy-intensive sectors,” Harry Chambers, an analyst at Capital Economics, said in a note.

“We wouldn’t conclude that the German economy has turned a corner and we still expect high energy prices to take a toll.”

So far, Merz’s government seems sanguine.

The Bundesnetzagentur, the government body that regulates gas, has said that “the risk of a tight gas supply continues to be low”.

The agency did “take very seriously” the low gas storage levels but it was up to the industry to “prepare for the winter and… take adequate precautions”.

Germany’s policy is to let the private sector sort out the storage and supply. But the problem, explains Arturo Regalado, from the energy analysis firm Kpler, is that the Iran war has turned the market upside down.

Almost since the war began, traders have expected normal shipments of Qatari gas via the Strait of Hormuz to resume quickly.

On that basis, they have set the futures price for gas that will be shipped in midwinter at a lower level than the price for today’s gas, which is still skewed higher by the closure of Hormuz.

“For storage operators, it’s not economic,” Regalado says. “In this market you cannot say, ‘Let’s store gas today and sell it higher later’. So it doesn’t incentivise the storage.”

The other challenge is that Asian buyers, who were more reliant on Qatar, are outbidding the Germans for American liquefied natural gas.

“The LNG market is tighter than you would expect going into summer. Throughout the summer, there was very strong competition between Europe and Asia for cargos,” Regalado says.

He’s pretty confident that, even at lower storage levels, Germany will still be able to buy and supply all the gas its industry and households need. But he admits that it’ll come with a painful price tag.

Merz’s popularity is even lower than Sir Keir Starmer’s was. If households start to feel the squeeze, he may be tempted to raid the public funds and offer price caps or bill discounts.

“There’s a playbook there but it’s not a great one. It’s expensive for any government to cushion the impact of high energy prices and it can blunt the signal that you should really be sending to people about conserving energy,” says Albert Cheung, the head of Bloomberg NEF.

Although Germany’s public finances aren’t as stretched as those of France or Britain, there is growing disquiet about the country’s persistent budget deficit.

German 10-year government bond yields, which indicate the market’s confidence in Berlin’s fiscal position, are at their highest since the eurozone crisis of 2011.

Merz has not extended the fuel tax cuts he brought in early in the Iran war, when petrol and diesel prices spiked. This, Brzeski says, would be the blueprint for any help with energy bills.

“The government has learned and would not provide a lot of support. It would be short-lived, if any at all,” he says.

The regulator has advised households to “use gas sparingly” while prices are high.

But if the cold starts to bite, Merz’s resolve will be tested – especially if he goes into winter having lost key state elections to the populist Right-wing party Alternative für Deutschland.

In that case, he may yet look at the sick man of Europe and reach for the fiscal defibrillator.

data.title: New green levy to drive up household energy bills
data.description:
Labour is set to load a new green levy on to household energy bills to help subsidise hundreds of millions of pounds for clean hydrogen projects.

The gas shipper obligation (GSO), which will be introduced in 2027, will initially add up to £7.10 to average gas and electricity bills.

The money raised will be used to fund an initial round of 10 green hydrogen schemes, aiding Labour’s efforts to replace fossil fuels with clean power.

Another 27 projects have already been shortlisted, meaning the levy’s costs will keep rising to fund them.

The GSO will also join a raft of other green levies being added to power bills, threatening Andy Burnham’s pledge to tackle the cost of living crisis by reducing household energy costs.

The Prime Minister has vowed to save families £45 a year by removing VAT from electricity bills but these savings are set to be wiped out by Ofgem’s price cap, which will rise by £60 from October.

Britain’s biggest energy companies have frequently blamed green levies as one of the main factors driving bills higher.

The GSO will start off small but its costs are expected to surge as green hydrogen production scales up to industrial levels.

It will be imposed on companies moving natural gas through the UK distribution system, which will then be able to recoup the costs from domestic and commercial energy bills.

A report from the Joint Office of Gas Transporters, an industry body, said: “The gas shipper obligation costs will ultimately be passed to consumers based upon their consumption so will have an effect on existing gas consumers and will entail a large number of consumers incurring this additional cost.”

The GSO money will fund the first “hydrogen allocation round (HAR1)”, under which an initial 10 trial schemes will get about £150m for projects to generate 115 megawatts (MW) worth of green hydrogen.

This is produced by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using renewable electricity. The hydrogen produced can then be used as a clean fuel.

The subsidy will be rapidly scaled up over successive allocation rounds in the same way that wind and solar have been expanded using a similar subsidy system.

Officials are already preparing to expand the GSO subsidy schemes to help fund more projects in the coming years.

In a second hydrogen allocation round (HAR2), households will help bankroll 27 projects with a capacity of 875MW.

Government documents show that subsequent subsidy rounds could increase this to 10 gigawatts (GW) – roughly equating to 10 of the UK’s existing nuclear power stations.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has not yet published any estimates of the impact of hydrogen subsidies on bills after HAR1 and refused to answer detailed questions on the programme.

However, industry experts suggest that hydrogen subsidies will eventually add around £40 to average annual domestic bills if the Government decides to commission the full 10GW of capacity.

The GSO will be in addition to the raft of other levies that collectively make up about 30pc of average domestic bills.

The Office for Budget Responsibility has warned that the green levies added to energy bills will rise from £10.5bn in 2025 to £18.5bn in 2030.

This is in addition to the sharp rises in standing charges needed to cover the estimated £110bn cost of upgrading UK grid networks by 2031.

David Turver, an analyst, said that electricity system prices – meaning the cost of subsidies and grid upgrades – were set to rise sharply over the next five years.

He added: “Green hydrogen is hugely expensive and there is no market for it.

“It is particularly perverse to subsidise something for which there is no demand and in the process further add to already high energy bills.”

The Low Carbon Contracts Company, which will collect the levy, described the GSO as “designed to incentivise investment in clean hydrogen production and usage”.

Richard Tice, the Reform UK energy spokesman, said: “Another day, another energy levy being added on consumer bills to pay for more speculative net-zero-related dreams. Reform will stop all this and remove these taxes and levies to slash bills.”

A DESNZ spokesman said: “Energy is an everyday essential and needs to be affordable for everyone, which is why we have cut VAT on electricity bills to give families breathing space.

“We will keep looking at what more we can do to protect households.”

data.title: I travelled the ‘border’ between North and South. Here’s what I learnt
data.description:
A sign by the estuary warns of danger, but it’s hard to see much to be afraid of here apart from the nettles and a fairly ominous sky. Under the Severn Bridge, on a spit of land on the river’s west side, it seems peaceful enough. Traffic roars overhead, but you can’t see the cars from below. There’s birdsong and the smell of wet foliage, glimmering water fringed by sodden sand and then cracked earth. It doesn’t feel like a border, but I’m standing at the far western end of England’s North-South divide.

There is, of course, no official line across England’s midriff. No razor-wire fences or passport checks mark where the South ends and the North begins. But nor is the boundary a figment of our imagination. We’ve heard enough jokes about the Watford Gap to know that Southerners see the North – the people, the places, the culture – as somehow different. And we Northerners, admittedly, can be bloody-minded about our Northern identity.

But how entrenched does the North-South divide remain today, after years of political talk of levelling up, Northern powerhouses and ill-fated high-speed rail connections? How much does our geography still shape how we see those from elsewhere in the country? And where, actually, does the notional dividing line start and end?

Apparently, not where you might expect. Recent YouGov data from almost 46,000 adults in England revealed that many people along the borders of the areas classified as North, South and Midlands don’t place themselves in the same regions government maps would suggest. Feelings of “Northernness” extended south of the regional borders, the pollsters found, while in the parts of East Anglia that supposedly sit in the South, people don’t all feel Southern. In short, like many types of identity, it’s complicated.

With that in mind, I have set out to travel along an unofficial boundary line between the North and South of England – one commonly used in academic research – to interrogate these feelings and explore what the divide means today. My editor has suggested I walk the entire 340 miles from Beachley Point on the Severn estuary to the Wash, between Lincolnshire and Norfolk, possibly in one go. I have counter-suggested the use of a motor vehicle.

The journey is a personal one. Having grown up in Leeds, my Northern identity is one I have insisted on throughout my adult life (which I’ve spent mostly in the South). When I started writing my debut crime thriller novel, The House on Otley Road, I knew it had to be set in West Yorkshire. Home.

The tug of the North has never left me, and I spend much of my time on the East Coast Main Line, travelling to and from where I spent my youth. But I’m surprised to find that it supposedly begins more or less where I’m standing by the Severn. The first (and only) person I encounter on the footpath here is Justin Charnock, 37. He identifies as Southern (this is fair – he comes from near Bristol) and thinks “people in the North are a lot nicer than people in the South” (also fair). “More welcoming,” he says.

It’s a commonly held perception, mentioned frequently by those I meet on my journey – almost all of whom have strong ideas about how Northerners differ from Southerners.

Charnock thinks being Southern traditionally means being “wealthier; a lot more aloof; snobby; much less hospitable, welcoming, friendly or helpful”. Working in the South West (he won’t divulge his job), he never gets tipped and “often people are a bit snooty”.

‘It’s become very middle class here’

Behind the popular images of Northerners lie some dispiriting numbers. The North East remains the region with the lowest healthy life expectancy at birth (HLE), at 57 years, according to the most recent figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). It has had the lowest HLE in every period since the ONS began measuring it. The South East remains the region with the highest HLE (63 years for men, 64.3 years for women).

A similar disparity can be seen in economic activity. In 2023, London had the highest gross domestic product per capita, at £69,077, while the North East had the lowest, at £28,583. It is worth noting, though, that the poverty rate is higher in London (26 per cent) than anywhere else in the country, according to figures from the charity Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

Meanwhile, perceptions of Northerners and Southerners that seem to stem from our economic histories – the North as industrial, the South as the country’s financial engine – have stubbornly persisted.

The first stop on my journey is Brockweir, a scenic Gloucestershire village on the river Wye. Old stone houses are painted in creamy yellow, pale blue and white, while green hills rise behind them. All the villagers seem to know each other. They all have dogs, and their dogs know each other too. The community owns its pub, the 16th-century Brockweir Inn.

“We tried to sell our bodies [to raise the money for it], but we’re all too old,” says Carol Knight, 76. (I think she’s joking.)

Her family has lived here for centuries. “It’s become very middle class,” says the suntanned, denim-dungaree-clad former English teacher, while clutching a bunch of Whitsuntide boss flowers and the leads of her two labradors. “Property prices have skyrocketed.”

Does this mean Brockweir must be Southern? House prices are, after all, a stark divider between North and South. Prices may be rising more steeply in the North at present, but the gap remains vast, even after removing London from the equation: in March 2026, the average house price across the South East and South West was £340,000, compared with £188,500 across the North East and North West.

‘We need more Northern leaders’

I travel onwards, trying to keep close to the Wye, down winding lanes bordered by verdant hedgerows and cow parsley. I stop at Upper Redbrook, where I can’t find a pub, or a shop, or a human, then Staunton, where the 18th-century pub isn’t open yet (it’s still too early). Traffic rattles through the village of silent modern houses.

In the Herefordshire village of Lea, I encounter a friendly pair of Scousers who decamped here long ago. Mike Tyson, a 46-year-old roofer and carpenter (“Yes, it’s my real name,” he says, for probably the millionth time), talks of his daughter’s “Northern attitude”.

What is it? “Friendlier, more easy-come, easy-go. ‘Chippy’ is the right phrase.”

The men are not the only ones to claim Northerners have a different (better?) sense of humour. But there’s uncertainty about whether we’re in the North or the South here – the consensus seems to be the middle – but Tyson believes there’s more money to be made down here than up in Liverpool.

Tied up with the question of economic activity and affluence is that of political power. Devolution to England’s cities and regions has given some control to communities far from Westminster. Whether it has helped those communities feel less overlooked is uncertain. Phil Henesey, 71, who is drinking in a beer garden with Tyson in the late-afternoon sunshine, says the North still feels farther (figuratively) from Westminster decision making.

“That’s why we need more Northern leaders,” he says.

He is speaking not long before the enthroning of a Northern leader in Downing Street. Andy Burnham, the Liverpool-born former Mayor of Greater Manchester, has made much of his links to, and concern for, the North of England. The new PM has created a No 10 North. In doing so, he has set himself up to be judged on how successfully he makes Northerners feel more connected to the centre of power. Also on how he does this without alienating the South.

‘There’s more chivalry in the North’

It’s raining when I reach Ledbury, the sky a grey-white sheet. The Tudor buildings are picture-perfect and well preserved. “It’s very much Middle England,” says a shopkeeper on the high street who doesn’t want to be named. “Did you ever see Keeping up Appearances? It’s full of Hyacinth Buckets [here].”

He identifies as a Southerner. “When you go up North, it’s dark,” he says. “It’s a funny old thing, that divide.”

Declan Butler, a 68-year-old Irishman who moved to Britain in the 1970s and now runs a gift shop down the road, thinks Ledbury is “probably more Southern”, judging by its disposable income.

“I had a couple in here from North Yorkshire at the weekend and they spoke to me as if we were old friends, whereas people from the South East are much more reserved,” he says. “If I was to choose a Southerner or a Northerner to be friends with, I’d choose a Northerner, because they’re friendlier. They’re probably harder workers. They’re grafters.”

He concedes that Cockneys and people from Essex can be friendly, too. Has he been to the North much? “I’ve been to Birmingham,” he offers.

Crossing into Worcestershire, I see the grey-blue shadow of the hills rise up ahead. I pass an old roadside chapel and an abandoned filling station, and arrive at Bredon, where the local Spar sells cider on tap.

“I thought the North started at Crewe,” muses Steve Fowler, an ex-Army man, inside the still-quiet Royal Oak pub, where there’s horse racing on the TV. He’s surprised to hear that by some definitions he is in the North right now. A Southerner by birth (Surrey), he awards the North another point for humour. “The funniest comedians are Northerners,” he says.

“I think [people] are more materialistic in the South,” says David Gray, a semi-retired gardener from Scotland. “There’s a lot more chivalry in the North.”

“It’s all about survival in the North,” chips in Paul Sefton, a retired butcher. He came here from North Wales 30 years ago “purely because someone said to me my kids would never get a proper job up North”.

‘The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties’

The North-South divide has been with us for a long time, chronicled and perpetuated by our art and culture. Elizabeth Gaskell’s North and South (published 1855) contrasts England’s tranquil, idyllic South with a grimy industrial North plagued by poverty and suffering. Almost 150 years later, David Peace evoked a dark and lawless North in his fictional Red Riding quartet. There was always something harder and edgier about the most famous Northern bands than their Southern counterparts. Contrast the Beatles with the Kinks, Oasis with Blur.

Yet in today’s hyperconnected society, how long can such differences last?

“It’s flattened out quite a bit by sheer mobility,” says Steve Fowler. And, he says, by exposure to the internet. “You would have to go very deep into the countryside, to very isolated communities, to find residual differences.”

In the Plough Inn in Stretton-on-Fosse, Warwickshire, Gordon Everett, 59, says, with both sadness and pride, “This is one of the last old-fashioned drinking pubs.” Local accents are waning a lot, he says, touching on the most overt marker of Northern or Southern identity. When he was a boy, you could tell the difference in accents between people from two local villages that lay just three miles apart. “Now, everyone’s got this flat English accent.”

Non-locals, he says, have come to the area and changed it. “The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties.”

Still, tracing this line across the country is a lesson in the extent to which our villages and small towns either cling to their past or else are haunted by it. Between Bredon and Stretton-on-Fosse, I pass houses with names such as the Old Bakehouse, the Old Stoves. A croquet club and a country clothing store. Less picturesque: a dead badger on the A44.

In Brackley, Northamptonshire, there’s a similar nostalgia in evidence. On the high street, there’s the Old Bakery and the Old Hall Bookshop. The sign for Brackley Community Shops is painted in old-fashioned fairground colours. One of these shops offers tattoos, but still.

In the Courtyard Shops farther along, I’m reminded of one of those mock-Victorian streets you find in museums, except there’s a vape shop here. Browsers are welcome, says a sticker in the window, and they’re also on CCTV.

A 75-year-old woman I meet in the town, when I ask what Northerners are like, suggests they’re either industrious farmers or else they work in “industrial places”. I don’t have the heart to tell her that no one I know in West Yorkshire does any such thing.

Did you know Brackley is in fact north of the North-South divide, I ask Anne Mellor, a volunteer in a local charity shop? “No,” she says, “we thought we were in the middle, surrounded by HS2.”

Depending on where you are in the North, transport links can be a sore point – and another marker of difference from the South. Burnham might be proud of his re-regulated Bee Network buses in Manchester, but raise the subject of the still-non-existent tram service in Leeds and that fabled Northern grit might give way to heavy sighs of Northern frustration.

In the North East, poor transport links were said last year to put more than 30 per cent of the region at risk of poverty. In 2022, lack of transport connectivity was found by the Centre for Cities to cost the North £16bn a year in productivity losses. Against this backdrop, HS2 has become a punchline, not an answer.

‘They’re parochial and territorial’

I’m travelling to Silverstone, Northamptonshire, which is famous for a different sort of transport. Pictures of motor-racing heroes adorn the walls of the village pub, the White Horse. I pass through a familiar landscape of roundabouts and roadworks before arriving. A poster on the village noticeboard invites me to become the best version of myself. (I decline.)

Gary Baird, 38, who runs the pub, thinks the North is more working class, while the South attracts more tourism. No one, he argues, goes to Hull on holiday.

Onwards to Rushden, Northants, a “historic boot and shoe town”, passing en route an American diner, a Starbucks, a Travelodge, a McDonald’s, a Toby Carvery and a new-build housing estate. I could be anywhere now. I don’t know whether I’m North or South, my senses are scrambled, or numbed by the dreary uniformity of our in-between spaces.

But in Rushden, for the first time, I feel I could be in the North. Behind the bar in the town’s Working Men’s Club, 30-year-old Tomethia Bartley confirms, “They’re Northerners here.” (She’s not – she’s from London.) “They’re all in a community together. Everyone knows everyone.”

She’s wearing a T-shirt saying, “Don’t like me? F--- off. Problem solved.” I don’t know how Northern or Southern this sentiment is.

Howard, 67, a former helicopter pilot enjoying a pint in the club with his partner, Lynette Keirnan, says: “I was married to a woman from Lancashire. She was bloody weird, actually. They seem to see things differently up there. They’re very parochial and territorial.

“They eat food like barm cakes [a bread roll from the North West] and black peas,” he adds. “They feel disenfranchised, I think.”

But out on the high street, it doesn’t feel so different here from many post-industrial towns further North, with grand old Victorian buildings and the sense of better days being behind it. There’s a kebab shop and an amusement arcade now. A nail bar, a Poundstretcher and, curiously, a large reptile specialist called House of Venom.

Deeply ingrained perceptions

The land flattens out as I enter Lincolnshire, stopping briefly in Market Deeping for a scalding portion of battered fish. “Sunny days are here at last,” it says on a small blackboard inside the Market Gate Deli. Outside, a fine rain falls. An unseasonable chill hangs in the early June air.

My odyssey ends in Norfolk, where I meet arable farmer Richard Ward, 55. “Where am I?” I ask.

“You’re probably North more than anything, because that’s the North Sea,” he says, pointing to the horizon, where I can’t see anything but farmland. A few years ago, a bomb squad came to remove a load of Second World War ordnance found in the fields. “It was quite a hairy experience,” says Ward.

Do people fish out there? I ask, pointing vaguely to where the sea should be. No, he says. “It’s dead vegetation and horrible black, boggy clay soil.”

I finish my journey not far from this, by a soggy field overlooking some marshland. The sun has finally emerged. Some desultory wasps buzz above the glistening wet grass. A crow caws, a cockerel crows and my feet are becoming very wet.

The conversations I’ve had along my journey have shown that, despite our increasingly homogenised culture, perceptions of differences between Northerners and Southerners remain deeply ingrained. Perhaps we will always retain these in some form.

As Richard Collett writes in his book Along the Borders, “We carve landscapes apart to define our very sense of self and identity.”

I recognise this impulse. And I’m not going to claim it’s all grim down South, but I’ll always be Northern and proud.

The House on Otley Road by Rosa Silverman (£16.99, HQ/HarperCollins) is out now.

data.title: Britain’s green taxes are economic vandalism
data.description:
Britain has lost two oil refineries in little more than a year. Grangemouth closed in April 2025 and Lindsey followed in August, leaving just four operating sites: Fawley, Humber, Pembroke and Stanlow.

This matters far beyond the companies and workers involved. Liquid fuels still provide 47pc of Britain’s energy consumption, with the UK now forced to import significant volumes of the diesel and jet fuel it needs.

These fuels are essential for road freight, agriculture, construction and aviation and for which there are no substitutes available at scale in the near term. In 2025, we imported 15.5 million tonnes more petroleum products than we exported, the largest deficit since Britain became a net importer in 2013.

Yet government policy is actively making this situation worse.

Refineries are covered by the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), a system in which emitters of carbon dioxide must surrender carbon allowances against their emissions. They receive some allowances free, ostensibly to protect against “carbon leakage”, but not enough to cover what they emit.

Based on average carbon prices over the past year, my analysis suggests the four remaining refineries face a net ETS cash cost of around £200m a year. This means they face a cost disadvantage of £540m compared with refiners in countries which do not have carbon pricing regimes.

This might be defensible if the ETS were actually encouraging refiners to reduce their emissions. But there is very little left for it to incentivise.

Refining is extremely energy intensive, so these facilities have always had a strong commercial incentive to improve efficiency. European refineries have spent decades investing in heat integration, cogeneration and process optimisation because every unit of energy saved improves their margins. Significant efficiency improvements were being made long before emissions trading existed.

Beyond further incremental efficiency gains, there are few meaningful investments UK refiners can make to reduce their emissions today. Neither carbon capture nor hydrogen schemes are viable without government support, which has been discussed for years but not delivered.

So what does the ETS achieve?

It makes refining in Britain more expensive. That’s it. And if refining in Britain is more expensive, then fuels imported from countries that don’t impose carbon costs will be cheaper. These fuels will displace the more expensive products refined here.

Britain’s new carbon border adjustment mechanism is supposed to protect domestic manufacturers from this type of carbon leakage by applying an equivalent price to certain imported goods. But refined petroleum products are excluded; there is no plan to make a tanker of diesel or jet fuel arriving from India, the Middle East or elsewhere bear the carbon cost imposed on the British refinery it competes with.

And those overseas competitors are formidable. Many refineries in Asia and the Middle East are newer, larger and more sophisticated than ours, which were all built in the 1950s and 1960s. Some benefit from state support, preferential access to crude, lower labour costs and much cheaper energy. It would be hard to compete with them at the best of times, yet Britain handicaps its refineries further by imposing a carbon price many of their competitors do not pay.

This exposes the central fiction in our carbon accounting: closing a British refinery does not make UK demand for diesel or jet fuel disappear; it increases imports. The emissions are not eliminated; they are moved elsewhere. Total emissions rise because the somewhere else tends to have higher emissions and there are further emissions from transporting the products to the UK.

While the Government celebrates a reduction in UK territorial emissions, global emissions rise. That’s not decarbonisation; it’s economic vandalism that we stupidly boast about.

The problem extends beyond refining. We are losing huge swathes of our manufacturing industries because our energy costs are extraordinarily high, and we impose asymmetric carbon costs. It is time to ask whether the ETS serves any useful purpose at all.

Consider electricity. What investment is the carbon price supposed to incentivise? Clearly it does not encourage a switch to renewable generation because renewables require large subsidies to be viable. With the closure of Britain’s last coal power stations, the only large-scale carbon-intensive generation we have is gas. We cannot eliminate gas and still operate the grid securely with today’s technologies. As with refineries, carbon capture schemes are not currently viable.

So the ETS is just another tax levied on the power sector. But unlike refineries, power stations can pass this cost through to consumers, so it makes our bills higher and adds to the cost burden faced by businesses.

Carbon pricing was supposed to change investment decisions and encourage emissions reductions. But where economically viable emissions reductions are available, businesses already have powerful reasons to improve efficiency. No extra encouragement is needed. Where they are not available, adding an ever-higher carbon price does not make them magically appear.

Instead, in electricity it becomes another cost to households and businesses. In refining, it becomes another reason to close the plant and import the product instead.

Britain should stop confusing lower territorial emissions with decarbonisation. An environmental policy which exports emissions, destroys domestic industry, increases import dependence and raises global emissions is deeply irrational. It is time to ditch the ETS.
