data.title: Healey’s oil tax raid risks driving up energy bills, warns Ineos
data.description:
A fresh tax raid on the North Sea risks pushing up household energy bills, petrochemicals giant Ineos has warned.

The British company, led by billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe, said proposals being considered by Labour to squeeze oil and gas companies harder would simply result in “higher costs for consumers”.

This is because raising the windfall tax would further increase costs for domestic producers, prompting more of them to shut down their operations and making Britain more reliant on imports of foreign liquefied natural gas.

David Bucknall, the chief executive of Ineos Energy, said: “Extending the windfall tax beyond 2030 puts existing licensed, in-progress projects at risk of failure to complete planned production, therefore risking planned supply input to the UK energy economy.

“It would instigate massive decommissioning across the industry, reducing overall taxes paid to the Government and increasing carbon emissions, as the UK’s energy needs would have to be met through imports.

“A policy change resulting in less tax paid, fewer jobs, higher costs for consumers and higher carbon emissions would be harmful for everyone in the UK.”

Any increase in household energy bills would risk undermining Andy Burnham’s drive to “put more money in people’s pockets”.

Labour already taxes oil and gas profits at 78pc under an existing windfall levy which Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, previously extended from 2028 to 2030.

The policy – originally introduced under the Conservatives – has been blamed for an exodus of jobs and investment in the North Sea, as well as higher production costs.

However, The Telegraph last week revealed that John Healey, who replaced Ms Reeves as Chancellor in July, is looking at extending or increasing the levy again as ministers scramble to plug a £4.7bn hole in the public finances.

The suggestion has alarmed industry insiders, who argue that it will simply accelerate the North Sea’s decline.

Russell Borthwick, the chief executive of the chamber of commerce in Aberdeen, which represents companies such as BP and Shell, has warned that businesses are already being “forced to make incredibly difficult decisions about their future”.

Trade body Offshore Energies UK has also claimed a fresh change to the tax regime would “severely undermine investor confidence and energy security”.

The warning of higher energy bills comes as Mr Burnham is already struggling to fulfil his promise of easing the pressure on stretched household budgets.

The Prime Minister announced plans to scrap VAT on energy bills in his first policy announcement after entering No 10. The move is forecast to reduce bills by £45 a year from October.

But the impact has been largely cancelled out by soaring wholesale energy costs triggered by the war in Iran. Ofgem last month said that the energy price cap will rise by £60 a year from October, while analysts have warned of more painful increases in the new year.

Concerns about rising bills come as Britain’s net zero drive faces a broader reckoning.

The Conservatives will this week pledge to abolish the 2008 Climate Change Act, saying it has led to the deindustrialisation of Britain and left the country poorer.

Andrew Bowie, the newly appointed shadow energy secretary, will introduce on Wednesday a 10-minute rule bill to repeal the act and scrap the Parliament’s climate change committee.

He is expected to say: “This Act has done nothing to combat global emissions. It has led to the deindustrialising of Great Britain. It has increased people’s energy bills.

“And it has allowed Government to engage on the greatest con ever played on the British people.”

A Treasury spokesman said: “The Chancellor is fully focused on his priorities, to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode.

“As has always been the case, the Chancellor will set out decisions at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

data.title: Railways at risk as weeks of record-breaking heat damages soil
data.description:
Around 20 per cent of England’s railways are vulnerable to derailment because of this year’s record-breaking heat, experts have warned.

About a fifth of railways in the country are built on clay soil, which can become very hard when dry, causing them to shrink and crack – and for anything built on top of them to move or subside.

Roughly 1,800 miles of rails lie on clay ground in areas classed as having a high or very high risk of drought, nature investment fund Rebalance Earth has said.

Rebalance Earth shared its findings after two train derailments took place less than 24 hours apart. Last week, a service came off the tracks just outside Lewes, East Sussex, injuring 30 people. A day later, another train derailed in Wickford, Essex.

Both incidents are under investigation by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB), with experts looking into the effect of hot and dry weather on the railways.

Investigators are examining whether the East Sussex accident could have been caused by conditions making the ground shift, causing the rails above to buckle.

A picture released by the RAIB shows a visible buckle or kink in the rails that was visible 20 minutes before the derailment.

Prof Neil Entwhistle, of Rebalance Earth, warned that clay soils – including the ground under the tracks in Lewes – are especially vulnerable to shifting when they dry out after prolonged hot and dry conditions.

“The RAIB’s initial report notes that the railway at Lewes is built on clay and alluvium that are sensitive to changes in water content, with evidence that some ground movement had already occurred,” he said.

“Investigators also identified a track geometry irregularity on the approach to the derailment, meaning the rails had shifted or become uneven, with ground movement being one potential cause,” he added.

The British Geological Survey has described the clay shrink–swell cycle as “the most damaging geohazard in Britain today”, warning that it can cause subsidence in houses as well as tens of millions of pounds in insurance claims.

Prof Entwhistle and Gabrielle Edghill, a geospatial analyst, graded each area of clay across the country for its drought risk, assigning them ratings between “very low” and “very high”. They then cross-referenced this model with the locations of all 10,000 miles of railway lines in Great Britain.

Ms Edghill said: “Uneven shrinkage beneath a railway can alter the position and level of the track, potentially creating an irregularity that requires speed restrictions, tamping or other intervention.”

There are a number of places in Britain where clay is the dominant type of ground. Most notably, this includes London, which is where the name of the colour “London Clay” originates.

Other types of clay include Wealden, Wadhurst, Oxford and Mercia Mudstone and there are various railway lines laid on top of those soils across southern England. However, not every railway line laid in a clay area is necessarily built on a clay embankment.

The Victorian engineers responsible for building the railways favoured these flat, low-lying grounds because it kept construction costs down.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, reportedly asked rail bosses whether anything “needed to be done across the network as a whole” after the incident in Wickford.

As reported by Rail magazine, Lord Hendy, a rail minister, said: “The Secretary of State asked on Friday afternoon [Aug 14] the most senior people in Network Rail, the operator, and the ORR [Office of Rail and Road] whether or not there was anything as a consequence of having two instances in a very short space of time that needed to be done across the network as a whole.”

Greater Thameslink Railway, which operates Southern-branded trains across the south of England, said earlier this week that the line between Lewes and Haywards Heath would not reopen until Sept 1.

A Network Rail spokesman said: “We have a range of techniques for managing drying clay around the railway.

“These include using technology to monitor our tracks and trackbed, maintaining the lineside to minimise water-hungry trees, and most importantly, preparing for summer with a programme of targeted track maintenance.

“With that work and the £2.6bn we are investing in climate resilience, our railway will be safe and reliable for years to come.”

data.title: Gas prices hit three-year high as UK reserves fall to lowest in Europe
data.description:
Gas prices have hit a three-year high just as new figures show UK reserves are amongst Europe’s lowest, prompting fears of a difficult winter.

European natural gas prices hit €75 (£64.38) per megawatt hour on Wednesday, the highest level since January 2023.

Prices have risen as hostilities between the US and Iran have reignited, threatening to extend the disruption to liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies from the Gulf.

Analysts warned that prices were set to rise further in the weeks before Europe begins to refill its storage facilities to prepare for winter.

Gas storage levels across the Continent were 63pc full in the last week of August, well below the 80pc average for this time of year and amongst the lowest levels ever recorded for this time of year.

Britain’s stocks are even lower, prompting warnings that the country may be forced to pay through the nose to secure supplies over winter.

The UK’s gas storage network is only 31pc full and contains three gigawatt hours (GWh) of fuel in storage, according to data from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas.

For comparison, Germany has 131 GWh of gas – about 44 times more than the UK. Even this level of supply is causing alarm in the country.

David Lewis, of energy market consultancy Wood Mackenzie, said Britain and Europe’s best hope was for a warm winter.

“Low storage levels and continued tightness in the global LNG market leave Europe with little buffer against further supply disruptions or demand spikes,” he said.

“Only under a mild winter scenario do we see scope for prices to fall from current levels. In almost all other scenarios, we would expect higher prices and increased volatility.”

Montel analytics warned that European gas prices could jump by 19pc this winter.

Higher prices mean households and businesses risk even higher bills. Regulator Ofgem announced last week that typical annual household gas and electricity bills will rise by £60 from October, with another increase expected in January. The regulator blamed rising gas prices for the increase.

Natasha Fielding, an analyst at energy consultancy Argus Media, said: “Europe is on course to have its most depleted start-of-winter reserves in 15 years.

“Low storage increases the risk of a really big winter price spike, if Europe gets sustained cold weather or faces other unplanned supply disruptions.”

Britain ‘will lose vital protection’

The UK has always relied on the North Sea to provide supplies of gas through winter, so it has never built much gas storage.

However, Ed Miliband’s ban on exploration, plus Labour’s extension of the windfall tax, means North Sea gas output has plummeted.

Britain has also cut support for its only major gas storage facility, the Centrica-owned Rough field in the North Sea, leaving the UK reliant on shipments of LNG bought on global markets.

A Centrica spokesman confirmed that the Rough storage facility was almost empty and called on Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, to make a decision about its future.

“Without a decision, Rough will be almost empty by winter and will close early next year. The country will lose vital protection against global energy shocks forever.”

Jean-Paul Harreman, the director of Montel, said the Continent’s failure to fill its storage was “remarkable after a long hot sunny summer when Europe burned far less gas than normal”.

Many countries resisted refilling storage in the hope that the Gulf crisis would come to an end and prices would fall, making it cheaper to stockpile.

Mr Harreman warned that this over-optimism would hit consumers hard. He said: “This has left storage below the EU’s required levels, with member states on track to miss the winter storage targets. Consumers may pay the price.”

data.title: Jim Ratcliffe’s bet on Denmark shows Britain how to save the North Sea
data.description:
From the cabin of a helicopter, the Nini West oil platform doesn’t look like much.

Like many other structures of its kind, Nini’s red-painted, rusting metal emerges from the North Sea, 150 miles off the Danish coast, where it has pumped fossil fuels for decades.

But this platform is now ground zero for a new multibillion-pound industry.

Rather than extracting millions of barrels of oil and gas that make a small but significant contributor to climate change, Nini is going into reverse.

Instead of pumping oil upwards, it will soon start flowing CO2 downwards – back into the Earth’s crust for permanent storage.

Sixty metres below sea level, the two wells that once produced oil have been re-engineered to carry waste gas 1,800 metres down, where it will be trapped forever under impermeable bedrock.

When it starts up this month, it will become the North Sea’s first commercial carbon capture and storage (CCS) facility – eventually burying eight million tonnes of CO2 a year.

For Denmark, it will be a green triumph. But for Britain the project marks another net zero humiliation.

Not just because the UK has spent a quarter of a century promising to “lead the world in carbon capture”, only to find itself beaten to the post by little Denmark.

The additional salt in the wound is that Ineos Energy, which is leading Nini West’s regeneration, is a British business that tried and failed to deploy similar schemes at home.

Ultimately, bureaucracy and costs forced them to look elsewhere.

Low carbon dreams

Denmark’s King Frederik has summoned Britain’s ambassador to join him at the opening of Project Greensand, as the Ineos CCS scheme is known, on Sept 18.

The Danish minister leading the project hopes a UK minister will attend, though suspects this is unlikely owing to Britain’s lack of involvement.

If they were to turn up, they’d see exactly what they’re missing.

To serve the Nini West platform, Ineos will deploy Carbon Destroyer 1.

This is a ship commissioned by Sir Jim Ratcliffe that will depart Denmark’s Esbjerg harbour to pump 5,300 tonnes of liquid CO2 into rocks deep under the North Sea.

It will be the first of many such voyages and perhaps the first of many such ships.

Sir Jim, Ineos’s founder and chief executive, envisages an eventual fleet of vessels taking CO2 offshore for deep subsea burial.

“We are creating a new waste disposal system for Europe,” says David Bucknall, the chief executive of Ineos Energy.

Ineos’s control room for the carbon-storage project lies on a second platform, Siri, a few miles from the Nini West structure.

There, Bucknall is carrying out final checks with his staff before the first commercial CO2 cargo arrives.

He and his team have spent the last few years building the value chain that will make collecting waste CO2, compressing it to a liquid and then pumping it underground, a profitable business.

The chain starts on Denmark’s industrial-scale pig and livestock farms – which are under increasing pressure to deal with the vast quantities of manure they produce.

Left to its own devices, manure decomposes to produce methane. This is another climate destroyer if it escapes, but it is one that can also be burnt to produce heat or electricity if caught and utilised.

Denmark now sources about 40pc of its natural gas and up to 4pc of its electricity from this biomethane.

Bucknall has done deals with Danish farm operators to collect the CO2 generated from biomethane.

“The farmers collect the manure, put it into an anaerobic digester to get methane, which is combusted, and then they collect the CO2, compress it and send it to us,” says Bucknall.

It means the farmers can offer the world not just low-carbon bacon but also green energy.

It also allows Ineos to sell high-quality carbon credits to the likes of Microsoft or Amazon, who can offset it against the emissions from data centres.

It sounds like a virtuous circle, provided the CO2 really can disappear.

That’s where Ineos comes in.

‘Key to this project’

Several years ago it was faced with a problem – and an opportunity.

The problem was that output from its North Sea oil and gas platforms – centred on the Siri and Nini fields – was in clear decline.

Eventually that would mean spending millions of pounds to decommission them.

The opportunity lay in Denmark’s growing demand for carbon capture and storage as the only viable way of dealing with its agricultural emissions.

These are so huge that the country has little chance of reaching its planned 70pc emissions cuts by 2030 without CCS.

Ineos and its partner, Harbour Energy, offered to become Denmark’s CO2 waste-disposal service, with farmers and the government paying them to pump CO2 into former oil fields.

The deal would also save Ineos the cost of decommissioning.

“The key to this project was assembling the value chain,” said Bucknall.

“We had to get investment decisions from the emitters [farms and factories], from the mayor of Esbjerg, to build the harbour facilities and for building the high pressure tanks to store the CO2 in the port.”

Perhaps the biggest decision was to build a new ship capable of safely carrying 5,000 tonnes of CO2 from Denmark out to the Nini West platform each week.

Sir Jim commissioned the Royal Niestern Sander shipyard in the Netherlands to build the Carbon Destroyer 1, which recently arrived in Esbjerg.

The ship and port upgrades are estimated to have cost Ineos £130m – a lot of money, but a far cry from the £22bn that Britain has committed to CCS technology.

Such vast sums are being invested despite the fact that CCS technology has never been tried at scale.

However, the hope is that it will one day serve as a key pillar of global climate policy.

As in Denmark, UK eco-campaigners and government advisers, such as the Climate Change Committee, argue that CCS is a “necessity, not an option” for reaching net zero.

Opponents disagree, warning that the technology is unproven with massive energy demands that will pile yet more costs onto household bills.

The concept dates back to 1977 when Cesare Marchetti, an Italian physicist, published a seminal scientific paper suggesting that emissions from coal and gas-fired power stations could be buried underground as a partial solution to climate change.

Two decades later, Norway’s energy company Statoil – now Equinor – showed it was feasible by stripping unwanted CO2 from its Sleipnir platform and pumping it deep into subsea rocks.

In the UK, Tony Blair integrated CCS into climate policy, with his 2003 energy white paper recognising it as a “promising way forward”.

But what then became apparent were the substantial costs.

Heavy price tag

Capturing CO2 from the waste gases of power plants or factories before compressing and transporting it needs high temperatures, advanced engineering and lots of expensive energy.

That means CCS in Britain has been a pipe dream for three decades.

Gordon Brown’s government launched a £1bn competition to fund a commercial-scale CCS project on a coal-fired power station in 2007, but the initiative never got off the ground.

Ed Miliband tried again by offering £15bn in 2008 in his first stint as energy secretary.

This followed other unsuccessful attempts under David Cameron’s government in 2011 and 2015.

This lack of progress was in stark contrast to countries elsewhere.

The Northern Lights project took off in Norway last year, pumping an initial 1.5 million tonnes of CO2 per year under the seabed.

The partners in the joint venture, Equinor, France’s TotalEnergies and Shell, another British firm, plan to increase that to 6.5 million tonnes by 2028.

So what went wrong in Britain? The answer lies in a toxic mix of over-ambition, with a focus on large CCS projects, combined with excessive bureaucracy.

“We tried to set up a project in British waters, but the UK regulators blocked us,” says Bucknall.

His key point is that CCS costs a fortune if the infrastructure is custom-built, which is largely the approach taken in the UK.

The process becomes a lot cheaper if it uses existing kit, such as Nini West and Siri. It also means mistakes are cheaper.

For example, in the UK North Sea, Ineos proposed exploiting its existing Breagh gas platform, from which it already planned to lay pipes to open a new gas field.

A second set of pipes could, Bucknall suggests, carry CO2 the other way, taking it for permanent burial in a separate layer of rock. But the UK rules would not allow it.

“The regulators wouldn’t let us link gas extraction with CO2 storage,” he says. “They said they couldn’t mix up hydrocarbon extraction strategy with carbon capture strategy.”

That blockage also stems from the windfall tax that was imposed on the UK oil and gas industry in the wake of the energy crisis, which was reinforced when Labour came to power.

Problems were compounded by a ban on exploring for new oil and gas under Miliband, the former energy secretary, with a view to winding down the UK offshore industry.

Ineos was one of many energy companies last year that cut or halted investment in the UK after those changes, causing a wave of job cuts and growing reliance on imported oil and gas.

“I vehemently disagree with Ed Miliband, who I don’t think listened to his economics lectures at university,” says Bucknall.

What, then, has happened to the UK’s fledgling carbon capture industry?

Back in 2024, Miliband committed £21.7bn to another attempt to build a CCS industry in the UK.

The funding, spread across 25 years, targets two primary industrial hubs: the East Coast Cluster on Teesside and the HyNet Cluster covering Merseyside and North Wales.

The idea is for carbon-intensive industries in both areas to start capturing CO2, which can then be collected in a network of new CO2 pipelines and pumped deep into rocks under the North Sea.

However, much of the infrastructure is being custom-built.

Two years later, work has only just begun. This means that inflation has already driven the predicted nominal costs for the two projects to £29bn, according to the Government’s own figures.

The pay-off for all that investment could be a green and growing industry.

Construction is under way on three CCS projects, namely a cement plant on Merseyside, an incinerator in Cheshire and a gas-fired power station on Teesside.

Two new CO2 transport and storage networks are being built around Merseyside and Teesside.

The Carbon Capture and Storage Association said: “Our analysis suggests that the wider sector could unlock £26bn in private investment by 2030 and support 50,000 jobs.”

But the price is huge – and how long will it take Britain to catch up with Denmark?

Britain’s failed promises

Back in 2021, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) pledged that the UK would be burying up to 30 million tonnes of CO2 a year by 2030.

That target has since itself been buried.

The latest pledges suggest CCS “market creation” by 2030 with a “self-sustaining industry” by 2035 – but with no clear promises around tonnages.

It would, however, be unfair to blame Miliband for the UK’s failed promises on CCS.

The UK has had around 13 changes of energy secretary since 2008. That rapid turnover is part of the problem, with each new face meaning twists and turns in policy.

In Denmark, the success of CCS is largely credited to one minister, Lars Aagaard.

Unlike Miliband and his predecessors, Aagaard was already an energy professional, having previously headed the Danish Energy Association.

Unlike his British peers, the Danish political system allowed Aagaard to hold the energy portfolio for nearly four years between 2022 and 2026, long enough to see it through from plan to reality.

“Denmark had already approved CCS including funding before I became a minister so my job was implementing it,” he says.

“I focused on changing the planning rules and regulations and getting the agreements between industries and local authorities to let it happen.”

Aagaard also had wide political support. He says: “Our parliament is not like the UK system. It’s based on proportional representation, so collaboration is essential. We have maybe 10 parties, but we had a consensus of up to 80pc of the votes supporting CCS.”

So why did he select British companies to take the scheme forward? “We welcome trustworthy partners. I don’t really even see them as UK companies because the face that they show in Denmark is extremely professional and aligned with, you could say, Danish values,” Aagaard says.

The British projects are designed to be on a much larger scale than that of Denmark.

“We are delivering the first-ever industrial scale carbon capture projects in the UK supporting thousands of jobs across the country and reigniting our industrial heartlands,” said a DESNZ spokesman, who refused to answer questions on how CCS would be funded.

That refusal suggests political sensitivity – meaning at least some of these costs will be loaded on to energy bills. That fear is confirmed by the Carbon Capture and Storage Association, an industry body.

It said: “The Government’s current funding model is a combination of Exchequer support and consumer-funded levies.”

Back on the Siri platform, however, Bucknall sees a different funding problem: will the money the UK has set aside for CCS outlast future changes in government? Can Britain’s politicians rebuild the consensus needed for companies to make long-term investments that will survive general elections?

He isn’t confident.

As for Aagaard, he says that whatever happens with UK policy, Denmark would always be welcome.

“For us, carbon capture is something that has to be bigger than Denmark. We want other countries to store their CO2 with us,” he says.

“If the UK or anyone else needs us, we are already open for business.”

data.title: Britain is flogging off yet another beloved brand
data.description:
KitKats, created by Rowntree’s, are now made by Nestlé, of Switzerland. Cadbury’s Dairy Milk, and the rest of its brands, are now manufactured by Mondelēz International of the United States. Jaguar Land Rover is owned by India’s Tata, while even HP Sauce is now brought to your local greasy spoon cafe courtesy of Heinz Kraft.

We have long been used to some of the most beloved British brands being sold off to foreign conglomerates. Now it appears that Colman’s Mustard, and even Marmite, may join the list.

The Italians, the Americans and certainly the French would never allow their most valuable brands to be sold abroad in such a cavalier fashion. It is time Britain started protecting the few we have left, because very soon it will be too late.

There can be few more quintessentially English products than Colman’s. The fiery, tangy mustard goes perfectly with a full English breakfast, especially if your head is a little worse the wear after a heavy night, but it is hard to see it fitting any other kind of cuisine.

It emerged last week that Unilever is putting the brand up for sale as part of the clean-up of its sprawling empire. Bankers have been appointed to find a buyer for the brand as part of the wider deal to merge its food business with the American spice giant McCormick.

Apparently there is a risk of a “mustard monopoly”, given that it already owns the popular American brand French’s, although it is hard to believe regulators could really argue that Colman’s was really the same product as the insipid, tasteless yellow liquid created on the other side of the Atlantic. 

We will have to see what happens as the sale process gets under way. But whether it is a private equity firm or another food conglomerate the chances are that it will be sold abroad. Arguably Marmite will as well, given that McCormick will control the brand, although it will be majority owned by Unilever’s shareholders. Control of another celebrated brand will have left these shores.

There is no point in blaming Unilever for that. The company has been long overdue a radical overhaul after years of underperformance, when it seemed to care more about social activism than selling more soap or mayonnaise.

What happens to all the heritage wrapped up in the Colman’s brand? The mustard was created by Jeremiah Colman way back in the early 1800s, and by the 1820s it had become J & J Colman. From its Norwich base, it was one of the first great food brands of the industrial revolution, pioneering a model that was eventually copied all over the world.

Will all of that be preserved when one of the private equity firms gets its hands on it? Probably lots of promises will be made when the papers are signed, but they should be taken with a large pinch of salt (or mustard). Very few of those kinds of pledges are ever stuck to.

In reality, very few countries have been as happy as Britain has been to flog off their most valuable brands to anyone who feels like getting their chequebook out. Italy has its “golden powers regime” designed to protect assets of strategic national relevance. The United States has the Committee on Foreign Investment that can block deals, and there is little question the Trump White House would use it to stop the sale of Coca-Cola or Oreos.

And France of course, has laws to protect national assets, and in the past has used them to protect the yogurt manufacturer Danone from a foreign stake-holding. In most countries, the sale of a brand as historic as Colman’s would provoke a furious debate. Here in Britain we just let the investment bankers get on with hawking it around to the highest bidder.

That is not good enough. Sure, we all believe in a free market in corporate assets. But you hardly have to agree with Andy Burnham, with his student union tirades about “ending 40 years of neoliberalism” to wonder if the sell-off has not gone too far. After all, it is hard to see that any of the brands have been improved by their foreign owners.

Cadbury has lost much of the magic that once made it special. HP Sauce has, perhaps unsurprisingly, failed to conquer the world, while the less that is said about Jaguar Land Rover the better. If the foreign owner were taking all the heritage, and using it to build global mega-brands, with everyone from San Francisco to Shanghai queuing up for a bar of Dairy Milk, then it would be worthwhile. But it hasn’t happened.

Instead, ties with what were once their local communities have been weakened, and products have lost their identity. True, KitKats are still made in York, but Nestlé cut more than 400 jobs at the factory in April, while Cadbury’s closed its Bristol plant years ago. That might have happened under local management. But if we are being honest it would have been less likely.

It doesn’t have to work out like this. There is nothing wrong with Unilever selling Colman’s. But it would be perfectly possible for the Government to insist on a British buyer. There are plenty of food companies or UK based investors that might well be interested so long as the price was reasonable. In fact, there is one natural buyer.

Perhaps Unilever should be encouraged by ministers to sell it to Reckitt, the company that used to be known as Reckitt & Colman after it merged with J & J Colman in 1938. It is a well-managed business, with plenty of experience of running a portfolio of brands. And most of all, Colman’s would remain a British owned brand – which is exactly what it should be.
